Characterizing Underrepresentation when
Generalizing Causal Survival Estimates

Bolun Liu Affiliation: Johns Hopkins University    Sean McGrath Affiliation: Washington University in St. Louis    Yiren Hou Affiliation: Yale University    Elizabeth A. Stuart Affiliation: Johns Hopkins University    Harsh Parikh Affiliation: Yale University
Abstract

Randomized trial findings are routinely generalized to broader target populations to inform decisions in medicine and public policy. When the trial sample is misaligned with the target population, generalized effect estimates can yield suboptimal decisions. We characterize the target subgroups that are underrepresented in the trial cohort in time-to-event settings. Here, underrepresentation arises in two distinct ways: baseline underrepresentation, when a subgroup’s covariate profile is rare in the trial relative to the target, and time-varying underrepresentation, when differential censoring erodes a subgroup over follow-up. Existing diagnostics either conflate these mechanisms or apply only to the baseline case. We show that the asymptotic variance of the efficient generalizability estimator admits a decomposition in which only two terms can diverge as representation weakens: a sampling-weight term capturing baseline misalignment and a censoring-weight term capturing differential loss to follow-up. Underrepresented subgroups are therefore those with imprecise generalized estimates, and the larger of the two terms gives the responsible channel. We use this decomposition in TRACE (Temporal Rashomon Analysis of CEnsored data), which combines a self-normalized variance objective with a tree-based search to localize underrepresented subgroups, attribute each to baseline mismatch or censoring, and find the follow-up intervals where censoring drives the variance inflation. We solve the joint problem with a parametric dynamic program nested inside a Rashomon ensemble of near-optimal trees. In synthetic benchmarks, TRACE recovers the planted underrepresented regions, attributing each to its mechanism and locating the follow-up windows that drive time-varying underrepresentation. In a case study generalizing the National Job Training Partnership Act (JTPA) Study to U.S. JTPA-eligible adults, restricting to reliably generalizable subgroups narrows the 95% confidence interval for the refined estimand by 60%.

1 Introduction

Findings from randomized trials are routinely transported to target populations beyond the trial sample, a practice known as generalizability. Examples range from extending oncology-trial results to broader patient cohorts (Cole and Stuart, 2010; Westreich et al., 2017) to transferring policy-evaluation findings across regions (Hotz et al., 2005; Stuart et al., 2011), and in each case the goal is to estimate treatment effects that remain valid for the target population. This goal is harder to reach with survival outcomes, which accrue over time for individuals who may be lost to follow-up, and researchers have therefore extended generalizability methods to transport time-to-event effects (Dahabreh et al., 2020), estimate heterogeneous effects under censoring (Cui et al., 2023), fuse survival data across sources (Liu et al., 2025), and incorporate machine-learning-based estimators (Rytgaard et al., 2022; Westling et al., 2024).

As a running example, we use the National Job Training Partnership Act (JTPA) Study (Bloom et al., 1997; Abadie et al., 2002), in which eligible adult applicants were randomized to be offered or denied federal job-training services, so that its estimated effect on time-to-employment has strong internal validity. To extend the JTPA findings to a broader policy target, we consider a population sample from the Current Population Survey (CPS), which represents JTPA-eligible adults nationally (Flood et al., 2022; Center for Economic and Policy Research, 2019). Under the assumptions in Section 3, JTPA training is estimated to increase the probability of employment at any point during the 2424 months by 2.72.7 percentage points among U.S. JTPA-eligible adults. Despite the large trial sample size, however, the 95%95\% confidence interval (CI) of [−10.5,+15.9][-10.5,\,+15.9] percentage points is wide enough to include both substantial benefit and substantial harm, and so too wide to inform labor policy.

Generalizability of time-to-event trial findings can fail through two mechanisms: baseline underrepresentation, which occurs when a subgroup’s covariate profile is sparsely observed in the trial relative to the target, and time-varying underrepresentation, which occurs when differential censoring depletes a subgroup’s trial sample over follow-up. Both mechanisms are at work in the JTPA-to-CPS generalization (Section 7), where they widen the interval above in ways that cannot be detected from the point estimate alone.

To our knowledge, no existing diagnostic handles both mechanisms: the closest, Parikh et al. (2025), targets baseline mismatch alone in cross-sectional settings and conflates the two when extended to time-to-event outcomes (Section 2). A policymaker using the JTPA findings therefore cannot tell which target subgroups the trial can be reliably generalized to, why generalization fails for the rest, or when during follow-up precision is lost. We propose TRACE (Temporal Rashomon Analysis of CEnsored data), an interpretable diagnostic built around these three questions, which, when applied to JTPA-to-CPS, identifies the reliably generalizable population, attributes failures elsewhere to baseline mismatch or censoring depletion, and narrows the 95%95\% confidence interval for the refined estimand by 60%60\%.

Contributions.

We propose TRACE, a general framework for diagnosing subgroup-level underrepresentation in time-to-event generalizability settings.

  1. 1.

    We derive a variance decomposition that isolates baseline and time-varying underrepresentation as two unbounded factors, reducing subgroup diagnosis to identifying where those factors inflate variance (Theorem 1; Section 3.3).

  2. 2.

    To answer the which, why, and when questions, we cast diagnosis as a variance-minimization problem with a self-regulating constraint, whose optimum trims units and intervenes on person-intervals in the subgroups most affected by each failure mechanism (Theorem 2; Section 4.3).

  3. 3.

    We solve this optimization with a scalable parametric dynamic program nested inside an interpretable Rashomon ensemble of near-optimal trees (Breiman (2001); Algorithm 3).

2 Related Work

Generalizability: cross-sectional and survival. Generalizability and transportability of trial findings are well-studied in biomedical research (Hotz et al., 2005; Cole and Stuart, 2010; Stuart et al., 2011; Tipton, 2014; Westreich et al., 2017; Dahabreh et al., 2020; Colnet et al., 2022; Degtiar and Rose, 2023) and in the machine learning community under the names domain shift/adaptation (Sugiyama et al., 2007; Quiñonero-Candela et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2023), with parallel developments in semi-supervised learning (Testa et al., 2025; Hou et al., 2025). Across these literatures, weighted, outcome-regression, and doubly robust estimators dominate practice. Extensions to time-to-event outcomes are more recent: Wen et al. (2025) derive semiparametric inference for a multi-source PATE on time-to-event outcomes, which is the basis for our framework, and doubly robust and targeted estimators that accommodate machine-learning nuisances have been developed in parallel (Lee et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2025), including orthogonal survival learners for heterogeneous effects under censoring (Frauen et al., 2025), with applied demonstrations in oncology (Ramagopalan et al., 2022; Zuo et al., 2022). Although a few of these authors note that heterogeneity inflates variance, none target subgroup underrepresentation as a primary methodological object, and none distinguish baseline from censoring-driven depletion.

Underrepresentation and refined estimands. Methods that correct for distributional shift, such as group distributionally robust optimization (DRO) (Sagawa et al., 2020), are well developed, whereas less is known about where a shift reduces precision, and we are not aware of work on when during follow-up this happens. The closest precedent, ROOT (Parikh et al., 2025), uses a sparse-tree Rashomon set to diagnose baseline underrepresentation in cross-sectional generalizability settings via examination of variance. TRACE builds on this tree-based approach and extends it to (i) decompose variance into baseline and censoring channels, (ii) attribute each underrepresented subgroup to its mechanism, and (iii) locate the intervals where censoring drives the loss of precision in settings with longitudinal outcome follow-up.

3 Setup and Variance Decomposition

In this section, we identify two unbounded factors from the asymptotic variance of the efficient generalizability estimator that correspond, respectively, to the baseline and time-varying failure mechanisms of Section 1. The decomposition is the foundation of the diagnostic in Section 4.

3.1 Data and Estimand

Data are observed at discrete follow-up intervals t=0,1,…,Tt=0,1,\ldots,T. A binary source indicator SS marks each unit as trial (S=1S=1) or target (S=0S=0); baseline covariates XX are observed on every unit. Trial units additionally carry a binary treatment A∈{0,1}A\in\{0,1\} and a longitudinal censoring-and-survival history. For each tt, Ct=1C_{t}=1 if the unit is censored (lost to follow-up) by interval tt and 00 otherwise, and Yt+1=1Y_{t+1}=1 if the unit is still event-free (at risk) at interval t+1t+1 and 00 once the event has occurred; Yt+1Y_{t+1} is observed only when Ct=0C_{t}=0. Each trial unit ii contributes Oi=(Si=1,Xi,Ai,Ci,0,(1−Ci,0)​Yi,1,Ci,1,…,Ci,T−1,(1−Ci,T−1)​Yi,T),O_{i}=\bigl(S_{i}=1,\,X_{i},\,A_{i},\,C_{i,0},\,(1-C_{i,0})Y_{i,1},\,C_{i,1},\,\ldots,\,C_{i,T-1},\,(1-C_{i,T-1})Y_{i,T}\bigr), while target units contribute only (Si=0,Xi)(S_{i}=0,X_{i}). That is, treatment, censoring, and event histories are observed only for the trial cohort, and target units contribute baseline covariates alone; the censoring and survival quantities introduced below are therefore defined on the trial population (S=1S=1) and transported to the target through XX. For any generic time-indexed variable ZtZ_{t}, set Z¯t=(Z0,…,Zt)\bar{Z}_{t}=(Z_{0},\ldots,Z_{t}), Z¯t=(Zt,…,ZT)\underaccent{\bar}{Z}_{t}=(Z_{t},\ldots,Z_{T}), and let YTaY_{T}^{a} denote the potential survival outcome at horizon TT under A=a∈{0,1}A=a\in\{0,1\}.

Our estimand is the target population average treatment effect (PATE) on the survival outcome at horizon TT, τT=τT​(1)−τT​(0)\tau_{T}=\tau_{T}(1)-\tau_{T}(0) with τT​(a)=𝔼⁡[YTa∣S=0]\tau_{T}(a)=\mathbb{E}[Y_{T}^{a}\mid S=0]. Equivalently, τT​(a)=Pr⁡(YTa=1∣S=0)\tau_{T}(a)=\Pr(Y_{T}^{a}=1\mid S=0), so τT\tau_{T} is a contrast of survival probabilities under A=0A=0 and A=1A=1 at horizon TT in the target population of interest.

3.2 Identification

Following Wen et al. (2025), assuming consistency, treatment-assignment positivity, and treatment exchangeability, we require the following identification assumptions:

  1. A1.

    Censoring positivity in the trial. For each aa and each t≤T−1t\leq T-1, Pr⁡(Ct=0∣C¯t−1=0,Y¯t=1,A=a,X,S=1)>0\Pr(C_{t}=0\mid\bar{C}_{t-1}=0,\,\bar{Y}_{t}=1,\,A=a,\,X,\,S=1)>0.

  2. A2.

    Conditional exchangeability in censoring. For each aa and each t≤T−1t\leq T-1, Y¯t+1⟂Ct|(C¯t−1=0,Y¯t=1,A=a,X,S=1)\underaccent{\bar}{Y}_{t+1}\perp C_{t}\mid(\bar{C}_{t-1}=0,\,\bar{Y}_{t}=1,\,A=a,\,X,\,S=1).

  3. A3.

    Conditional exchangeability over SS. For each aa and each t≤Tt\leq T, Yta⟂S|(C¯t−1=0,Y¯t−1=1,A=a,X)Y_{t}^{a}\perp S\mid(\bar{C}_{t-1}=0,\,\bar{Y}_{t-1}=1,\,A=a,\,X).

  4. A4.

    Trial-participation positivity. If Pr⁡(X=x∣S=0)>0\Pr(X=x\mid S=0)>0, then Pr⁡(X=x∣S=1)>0\Pr(X=x\mid S=1)>0.

Together with the standard trial assumptions, A1–A2 identify the within-trial treatment effect on survival and A3–A4 transport it to the target (Dahabreh et al., 2020; Colnet et al., 2022; Degtiar and Rose, 2023), so A1–A4 suffice for point identification of τT\tau_{T} (formal statements and discussion in Appendix A). They do not, however, suffice for uniform reliability across the covariate space and across follow-up: A4 may hold globally yet be near-violated for specific covariate profiles, and A1 may hold globally yet be near-violated at specific covariate values and follow-up intervals. These near-violations are the two failure mechanisms of Section 1, and they appear in two identifiable quantities:

ℓ⁡(X)≡Pr⁡(S=0∣X)Pr⁡(S=1∣X),πC,ja​(X)≡Pr⁡(Cj=0∣C¯j−1=0,Y¯j=1,A=a,X,S=1).\ell(X)\equiv\frac{\Pr(S=0\mid X)}{\Pr(S=1\mid X)},\qquad\pi^{a}_{C,j}(X)\equiv\Pr(C_{j}=0\mid\bar{C}_{j-1}=0,\,\bar{Y}_{j}=1,\,A=a,\,X,\,S=1).

ℓ⁡(X)\ell(X) is large at covariate profiles common in the target but rare in the trial, a near-violation of A4 that drives baseline underrepresentation. πC,ja​(X)\pi^{a}_{C,j}(X) is small at person-intervals where remaining uncensored is unlikely; its inverse, the IPCW weight 1/πC,ja​(X)1/\pi^{a}_{C,j}(X), is correspondingly large, a near-violation of A1 that drives time-varying underrepresentation.

(2025), are derived in Appendices B and  D. We now state the central diagnostic identity of TRACE.

Theorem 1 (Variance decomposition).

Given A1–A4 and standard randomization assumptions, under a nonparametric model on the observed data, the asymptotic variance attaining the semiparametric efficiency bound is

where Wt−1a(O)=𝟏{S=1} 1{A=a} 1{C¯t−1=0}/{Pr(S=0)πa(X)}W^{a}_{t-1}(O)=\mathbf{1}\{S=1\}\,\mathbf{1}\{A=a\}\,\mathbf{1}\{\bar{C}_{t-1}=0\}/\{\Pr(S=0)\,\pi^{a}(X)\} denotes the trial-at-risk weight with πa​(X)=Pr⁡(A=a∣X,S=1)\pi^{a}(X)=\Pr(A=a\mid X,S=1), {Qja​(X)}j=0T\{Q^{a}_{j}(X)\}_{j=0}^{T} the iterated conditional survival probabilities, and τT​(X)\tau_{T}(X) the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) at horizon TT. Formal definitions, variance derivation, and proof of the worst-case bounds are in Appendix E.

Equation (1) has two kinds of factors. The green factors, i.e., bounded survival probabilities, the randomization probability, and design constants, are bounded (worst-case bounds beneath each box), whereas the red factors are not: ℓ⁡(X)\ell(X) inflates at baseline-underrepresented covariate profiles, and 1/∏j<tπC,ja​(X)1/\prod_{j<t}\pi^{a}_{C,j}(X) inflates at time-varying-underrepresented person-intervals. The two red factors map onto the diagnostic questions of Section 1, in that large values of ℓ⁡(X)\ell(X) mark which subgroups are underrepresented at baseline (the baseline why), and large values of 1/∏j<tπC,ja​(X)1/\prod_{j<t}\pi^{a}_{C,j}(X) mark when censoring depletes them (the temporal why). Characterizing underrepresented subgroups therefore reduces to localizing where the red factors inflate the variance most, a search problem that we formulate as a tractable optimization in Section 4.

What counts as underrepresented. We call a subgroup underrepresented when the trial cannot support a precise generalized estimate for it, i.e., when its contribution to the efficiency-bound variance in Theorem 1 is large. This decision-relevant notion (Rudolph et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023; Parikh et al., 2025) couples how rare a profile is in the trial with how much remains to be learned about it, so a large ℓ⁡(X)\ell(X) alone is not enough: ℓ​(X)2\ell(X)^{2} enters (1) only multiplied by the survival-increment variance [Qta​(X)]2−[Qt−1a​(X)]2[Q^{a}_{t}(X)]^{2}-[Q^{a}_{t-1}(X)]^{2}, and a profile that is rare in the trial but whose treatment effects are nearly deterministic (homogeneous) is estimated precisely from the few trial units available and is not flagged. A rare profile with variable treatment effects (heterogeneous) is flagged, because the generalized estimate there is imprecise and can change the treatment decision.

4 The TRACE Framework

Diagnosis therefore amounts to finding the covariate profiles and follow-up intervals at which the two red factors inflate the variance most, which we do in three steps. We first introduce two interventions, one per red factor, that contract the variance along its baseline and time-varying axes (Section 4.1). We then pose a bilevel optimization problem that minimizes the variance jointly over the two interventions, and provide the analytical and empirical objectives that make it tractable (Section 4.2). Finally, we read the optimum as a four-region partition of the data and use it to answer the which, why, and when questions of Section 1 (Section 4.3).

4.1 Two interventions: BB and hh

Baseline trim BB. Let B:𝒳→{0,1}B:\mathcal{X}\to\{0,1\} be a measurable function applied symmetrically to trial and target. Setting B⁡(x)=0B(x)=0 refines the estimand from the target PATE to the BB-restricted PATE τT(B)≡𝔼[YT1−YT0∣S=0,B(X)=1]\tau_{T}(B)\equiv\mathbb{E}[Y_{T}^{1}-Y_{T}^{0}\mid S=0,\,B(X)=1], with pB≡Pr⁡(S=0,B⁡(X)=1)>0p_{B}\equiv\Pr(S=0,\,B(X)=1)>0 and identified under A1–A4 restricted to {B(X)=1}\{B(X)=1\}. BB contracts the ℓ​(X)2\ell(X)^{2} red factor across covariate space, so that the retained set {B(X)=1}\{B(X)=1\} is the subpopulation to which the trial generalizes reliably (the which question).

Censoring intervention hh. Let hi,t∈{0,1}h_{i,t}\in\{0,1\} be a trial-side, person-interval indicator. Setting hi,t=1h_{i,t}=1 replaces unit ii’s observed law with the counterfactual law in which Pr(Ct=0∣⋅)=1\Pr(C_{t}=0\mid\cdot)=1 at interval tt, i.e., as if censoring had not occurred there. hh contracts the 1/∏j<tπC,ja​(X)1/\prod_{j<t}\pi^{a}_{C,j}(X) red factor across person-intervals, and the intervals with hi,t=1h_{i,t}=1 are those at which censoring depletion inflates the variance most (the when question). hh is thus both a diagnostic and a guide for future trials, since better retention or follow-up in the flagged subgroups and intervals would most improve precision.

Together, (B,h)(B,h) map each red factor to a distinct intervention, a correspondence we make precise in Theorem 2 below.

4.2 The TRACE objective

Bilevel optimization. The diagnostic we want is the joint (B,h)(B,h) that contracts the variance most. Because BB refines the estimand and hh refines the trial sample, we couple the two through a profiled bilevel problem:

B∗=arg⁡minB​V^​(B,h∗​(B)),h∗​(B)=arg⁡minh​V^​(B,h)+λh​‖h‖1.B^{*}\;=\;\arg\min_{B}\,\widehat{V}\!\bigl(B,\,h^{*}(B)\bigr),\qquad h^{*}(B)\;=\;\arg\min_{h}\,\widehat{V}(B,h)\;+\;\lambda_{h}\|h\|_{1}. (2)

The outer level chooses the baseline trim; the inner level returns, for each candidate BB, the censoring intervention that minimizes a sparsity-penalized variance. The remainder of the section gives the analytical form of V⁡(B,h)V(B,h), the empirical estimator V^\widehat{V} that plugs into (2), and the calibration of λh\lambda_{h}.

Analytical objective. The next theorem expresses the variance under (B,h)(B,h) as a parametric family containing Theorem 1’s expression as the no-intervention special case, and implies that BB and hh act on separate red factors.

+𝔼𝒫​[𝟏​{S=0,B⁡(X)=1}pB2​(τT​(X)−τT​(B))2].\displaystyle+\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}}\!\biggl[\,\hbox{\pagecolor{green!25}$\displaystyle\frac{\mathbf{1}\{S=0,\,B(X)=1\}}{p_{B}^{2}}\bigl(\tau_{T}(X)-\tau_{T}(B)\bigr)^{2}$}\,\biggr].

where χτT​(O,B)\chi_{\tau_{T}}(O;B) is the EIF for τT​(B)\tau_{T}(B) (Appendix F), 𝒫\mathcal{P} is the observed-data law, and 𝒫i∗\mathcal{P}^{*}_{i} is the counterfactual law for unit ii in which Pr(Cj=0∣⋅)=1\Pr(C_{j}=0\mid\cdot)=1 at every interval jj with hi,j=1h_{i,j}=1. In particular, V⁡(𝟏,𝟎)V(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{0}) recovers Var​{χτT​(O)}\mathrm{Var}\{\chi_{\tau_{T}}(O)\} from Theorem 1. Proof in Appendix G.

The red/green structure of Theorem 1 carries over to Theorem 2: the green factors remain bounded, while the two red factors are now under explicit control of the interventions. Setting B⁡(Xi)=0B(X_{i})=0 removes unit ii’s contribution from the trial sum, attenuating the average of ℓ​(X)2\ell(X)^{2} over the retained subpopulation; setting hi,j=1h_{i,j}=1 halves the exponent on πC,ja​(X)\pi^{a}_{C,j}(X) in unit ii’s contribution, attenuating the censoring product. Minimizing V⁡(B,h)V(B,h) over (B,h)(B,h) therefore works by shrinking the two unbounded factors we want to localize.

Attribution by intervention. The two red factors enter the variance multiplicatively, so the variance alone does not identify the baseline-vs-censoring split; TRACE attributes by intervention instead, using the variance only as the objective. Because BB changes only ℓ⁡(X)\ell(X) and hh only the censoring product (Theorem 2), we attribute a region’s inflation to baseline underrepresentation if trimming with BB removes it, and to censoring if hh does. Regions inflated on both axes are resolved by RR-gating: before any trimming, TRACE computes for each trial unit the ratio of its baseline to its censoring-driven variance inflation,

Ri=ℓ^​(Xi)2/Fi,R_{i}\;=\;\hat{\ell}(X_{i})^{2}/F_{i}, (4)

where Fi≥1F_{i}\geq 1 is the unit’s censoring-amplification factor (Appendix K); large RiR_{i} means baseline is the dominant cause and hh is suppressed for that unit; small RiR_{i} means censoring dominates.

Empirical objective. Plugging (3) into (2) requires an estimator of V⁡(B,h)V(B,h). We consider the block-self-normalized (mixed-Hájek) estimator

V^(B,h)=1n​(p^Btrl)2∑i:Si=1B(Xi)Ψ(Oi;hi)⏟trial block+1n​(p^Btgt)2∑i:Si=0B(Xi)(τ^(Xi)−τ^T(B))2⏟target block,\displaystyle\widehat{V}(B,h)=\underbrace{\frac{1}{n\,(\hat{p}_{B}^{\text{trl}})^{2}}\!\!\sum_{i:\,S_{i}=1}\!\!B(X_{i})\,\Psi(O_{i};h_{i})}_{\text{trial block}}+\underbrace{\frac{1}{n\,(\hat{p}_{B}^{\text{tgt}})^{2}}\!\!\sum_{i:\,S_{i}=0}\!\!B(X_{i})\,\bigl(\hat{\tau}(X_{i})-\hat{\tau}_{T}(B)\bigr)^{2}}_{\text{target block}}, (5)

with block-specific Hájek denominators p^Btrl=n−1∑i:Si=1ℓ^(Xi)B(Xi)\hat{p}_{B}^{\text{trl}}=n^{-1}\!\sum_{i:S_{i}=1}\hat{\ell}(X_{i})\,B(X_{i}) and p^Btgt=n−1∑i:Si=0B(Xi)\hat{p}_{B}^{\text{tgt}}=n^{-1}\!\sum_{i:S_{i}=0}B(X_{i}), where Ψ⁡(Oi,hi)\Psi(O_{i};h_{i}) is a functional of the trial data and hih_{i}, defined in Appendix H.

Two features of the proposed V^​(B,h)\widehat{V}(B,h) make the bilevel search practical. (i) Self-regulation. The squared Hájek denominator p^B−2\hat{p}_{B}^{-2} grows superlinearly as BB excludes more units, so each additional trim carries an internally generated cost. The optimum B∗B^{*} therefore removes a region only when its variance contribution exceeds that cost, so no explicit penalty on BB is needed (formal statement in Theorem I.1, Appendix I). (ii) Decoupling. The nuisance functions in (5) are fitted once from the full observed data, independently of (B,h)(B,h): changing BB only zeroes ℓ⁡(X)\ell(X) and rescales p^B\hat{p}_{B}, and changing hi,th_{i,t} updates a single interval’s πC,ja​(X)\pi_{C,j}^{a}(X) contribution. The bilevel search therefore avoids nuisance refitting altogether and can be decomposed into sub-optimization problems in Section 5.

Calibration of λh\lambda_{h}. The inner penalty λh\lambda_{h} is calibrated to a sparsity level η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1) rather than chosen as a free hyperparameter. At the no-trim baseline (B,h)=(𝟏,𝟎)(B,h)=(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{0}), define each hi,kh_{i,k}’s standalone variance reduction

Δ​V^i,k≔V^​(𝟏,𝟎)−V^​(𝟏,hi,k=1),\Delta\widehat{V}_{i,k}\;\coloneqq\;\widehat{V}(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{0})-\widehat{V}(\mathbf{1},\,h_{i,k}=1),

i.e., the drop in V^\widehat{V} from activating hi,kh_{i,k} alone. Set λh\lambda_{h} equal to the η\eta-quantile of Δ​V^i,k\Delta\widehat{V}_{i,k}. An hi,kh_{i,k} is then kept by the inner penalty iff Δ​V^i,k>λh\Delta\widehat{V}_{i,k}>\lambda_{h}, which by construction holds for exactly the top 1−η1-\eta fraction of person-intervals. With the default η=0.95\eta=0.95, h∗​(𝟏)h^{*}(\mathbf{1}) activates the 5%5\% of person-intervals whose standalone contribution to the censoring-driven variance is largest; the remaining 95%95\% are penalized out. We specify η\eta rather than λh\lambda_{h} because 1−η1-\eta is simply the fraction of person-intervals flagged.

4.3 Reading the optimum: a four-region partition

The optimum (B∗,h∗)(B^{*},h^{*}) and the gate RiR_{i} partition the target into four diagnostic regions, each with a distinct interpretation:

  1. (i)

    Reliably generalizable (B∗=1B^{*}=1, h∗=𝟎h^{*}=\mathbf{0}; which): subgroups whose trial estimates transport precisely to the target.

  2. (ii)

    Censoring-depleted (B∗=1B^{*}=1, h∗≠𝟎h^{*}\neq\mathbf{0}; temporal why and when): subgroups that are well-represented at baseline but lose precision through differential censoring; the indices (i,t)(i,t) at which hi,t∗=1h^{*}_{i,t}=1 give the follow-up intervals responsible.

  3. (iii)

    Baseline-underrepresented (B∗=0B^{*}=0, RiR_{i} large; baseline why): subgroups whose covariate profiles are too rare in the trial relative to the target, with censoring playing no material role, so that future trials could fix this region directly through recruitment.

  4. (iv)

    Doubly underrepresented (B∗=0B^{*}=0, RiR_{i} small; baseline and temporal why): subgroups that are both rare at baseline and depleted by censoring. Both interventions reduce their variance contribution, and RiR_{i} measures which mechanism dominates.

Since hh is not computed for trimmed units, (iii) and (iv) are separated by RiR_{i} rather than by h∗h^{*} (Appendix K.5).

In region (i) the trial supports a precise generalized estimate, whereas regions (ii)–(iv) need further data collection, in the form of better retention for censoring depletion, more trial participants with the rare baseline profiles, or both. For censoring-depleted subgroups, h∗h^{*} also gives the follow-up intervals where retention matters most.

5 Nested Optimization

The profiling identity in (2), along with the fact that the nuisance functions are independent of (B,h)(B,h), allows the bilevel optimization problem to split into two independent subproblems: an inner over h∈{0,1}ntrl×Th\in\{0,1\}^{n_{\text{trl}}\times T}, which we solve with a scalable parametric dynamic program, and an outer over B∈{0,1}𝒳B\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal{X}}, solved with an interpretable Rashomon ensemble of trees.

5.1 Inner: a per-unit affine envelope

For fixed BB, the trial block of V^​(B)\widehat{V}(B) decouples across units, so the inner problem reduces to a per-individual minimization. A short structural argument (Appendix J) further collapses the 2T2^{T}-way binary search over hi∈{0,1}Th_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{T} to a (T+1)(T{+}1)-way search over the integer ℓ1\ell_{1}-budget j=‖hi‖1j=\|h_{i}\|_{1}:

minhi∈{0,1}T⁡[V^i​(B,hi)+λh​‖hi‖1]=minj∈{0,…,T}⁡[αi​(B)​fi,j+λh​j],αi​(B)≔B⁡(Xi)n​(p^Btrl)2.\min_{h_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{T}}\!\bigl[\widehat{V}_{i}(B,h_{i})+\lambda_{h}\,\|h_{i}\|_{1}\bigr]\;=\;\min_{j\in\{0,\ldots,T\}}\!\bigl[\alpha_{i}(B)\,f_{i,j}\,+\,\lambda_{h}\,j\bigr],\qquad\alpha_{i}(B)\coloneqq\frac{B(X_{i})}{n\,(\hat{p}_{B}^{\text{trl}})^{2}}. (6)

Intuition. Two structural facts drive (6). (i) Budget sufficiency. Within the class of hih_{i} sharing a common ℓ1\ell_{1}-budget jj, the penalty λh​j\lambda_{h}j is constant and only the variance contribution varies; partitioning {0,1}T\{0,1\}^{T} by budget reduces 2T2^{T} candidate configurations to T+1T{+}1 representative slopes {fi,j}j=0T\{f_{i,j}\}_{j=0}^{T}, each the budget-jj minimum of the variance contribution alone. The right-hand side of (6) is then a lower envelope of T+1T{+}1 affine functions of the scalar αi​(B)\alpha_{i}(B). (ii) Decoupling. The slopes fi,jf_{i,j} are functions of the fitted nuisances and the budget alone, i.e., BB enters (6) only through αi​(B)\alpha_{i}(B), so the slopes are independent of every candidate BB the outer ensemble visits.

Computational gain. Each fi,jf_{i,j} is the optimum of a (Tj)\binom{T}{j}-way subset selection, but the additive cumulative state of the censoring product (Appendix J) admits a budget-augmented Bellman recursion that returns all T+1T{+}1 slopes in 𝒪⁡(T2​G)\mathcal{O}(T^{2}G) time per unit on a state grid of size GG, with grid error vanishing as G→∞G\to\infty (Theorem 3). Decoupling lets us precompute the slopes once at 𝒪⁡(ntrl​T2​G)\mathcal{O}(n_{\text{trl}}\,T^{2}\,G) total cost; each subsequent outer query of BB then reduces to walking the per-unit envelopes at 𝒪⁡(ntrl​T)\mathcal{O}(n_{\text{trl}}\,T), a factor of 𝒪⁡(T​G)\mathcal{O}(TG) faster than a non-parametric DP that absorbs αi​(B)\alpha_{i}(B) into the recursion and rebuilds at every BB. This precomputation makes the joint search over an ensemble of MM trees practical. In total, growing MM depth-DD trees over FF covariates costs 𝒪⁡(ntrl​T2​G+M​ 2D​F​ntrl​T)\mathcal{O}(n_{\mathrm{trl}}\,T^{2}G+M\,2^{D}F\,n_{\mathrm{trl}}\,T): the expensive T2​GT^{2}G build is paid once and never compounds with the 2D2^{D} tree term (Appendix Q).

5.2 Outer problem: Rashomon ensemble of trees

Given h∗​(B)h^{*}(B), we optimize BB via the Rashomon Set of Optimal Trees (ROOT) algorithm of Parikh et al. (2025). ROOT is designed for variance-style objectives that depend globally on the current partition rather than additively on its leaves, a structure that, to our knowledge, other tree methods do not accommodate. The obstacle for off-the-shelf alternatives is that V^\widehat{V} is not branch-additive: flipping a single leaf of BB rescales the Hájek denominators p^Btrl\hat{p}_{B}^{\text{trl}} and p^Btgt\hat{p}_{B}^{\text{tgt}}, which multiply every leaf’s contribution, so any greedy learner that scores splits against branch-local quantities (CART (Breiman et al., 1984), MOB (Zeileis et al., 2008), causal forests (Wager and Athey, 2018)) optimizes a different objective. ROOT instead scores every candidate split against V^​(B)\widehat{V}(B) on the full data: MM randomized trees are grown over the union of trial and target individuals, each split is accepted only if it lowers the global V^​(B)\widehat{V}(B) on the current partition, the top-KK trees within tolerance of the best objective form the Rashomon set (Breiman, 2001), and B∗B^{*} is aggregated by majority vote across that set. The aggregated B∗B^{*} can be summarized as a decision tree over baseline covariates, so the which answer of Section 4.3 can be audited directly.

We summarize the full nested procedure in Algorithm 3 (Appendix L).

6 Experiments

We apply TRACE to synthetic settings with baseline and time-varying underrepresentation, in which Experiment 1 combines both mechanisms with ten covariates and Experiments 2a–2d isolate each mechanism and include an adversarial case (details in Appendix M).

Experiment 1. Ten i.i.d. 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1) covariates are generated, where X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} affect trial-participation and survival, X3X_{3} and X4X_{4} affect censoring, and X5,…,X10X_{5},\ldots,X_{10} are noise. The censoring structure creates two subgroups: high X3X_{3} (but not X4X_{4}) produces an early modest spike in censoring at t∈{3,4,5}t\in\{3,4,5\} and high X4X_{4} (but not X3X_{3}) produces a late heavy spike at t∈{7,8,9}t\in\{7,8,9\}. TRACE recovers the underrepresented subgroups (Figure 1): B∗B^{*} trims on {X1,X2}\{X_{1},X_{2}\}, while h∗h^{*} activates almost exclusively on individuals in the two censoring-spike subgroups defined by X3X_{3} and X4X_{4}, with the noise covariates unused by either intervention. The two spikes are recovered at the correct intervals, and h∗h^{*} activates comparable numbers of person-intervals in both subgroups despite the late spike’s larger peak hazard, consistent with the greater downstream impact of early censoring.

Experiment 2a: Baseline underrepresentation only. ℓ⁡(X)\ell(X) depends on X1X_{1} and the censoring probability is negligible in this experiment. TRACE correctly trims the region with high values of ℓ\ell and does not invoke hh (Figure 2, column 1).

Experiment 2b: Time-varying underrepresentation only. Here ℓ⁡(X)\ell(X) is negligible and censoring spikes at t=3t=3 when X2<0X_{2}<0, so TRACE trims only a thin region and intervenes on every hh recipient at t=3t=3 and nowhere else (Figure 2, column 2).

Experiment 2c: Baseline and time-varying underrepresentation. This experiment combines 2a and 2b, with trial participation depending on X1X_{1} and censoring spiking at t=3t=3 when X2<0X_{2}<0. Because the two mechanisms act on independent covariates, both trimming and hh-targeting are needed, and TRACE trims the high-ℓ\ell tail on X1X_{1} while h∗h^{*} activates on individuals with X2<0X_{2}<0 at and around t=3t=3 (Figure 2, column 3).

Experiment 2d: Adversarial case for TRACE. In this experiment, the trial-participation odds are low (so that ℓ⁡(X)\ell(X) is high) in two off-diagonal corners of the (X1,X2)(X_{1},X_{2}) plane, a structure no single axis-aligned split can exactly recover, while censoring spikes when X1+X2<0X_{1}+X_{2}<0 at time 33. TRACE trims the two high-ℓ\ell corners rather than a half-plane, and h∗h^{*} activates almost exclusively at t=3t=3 among the retained trial individuals (Figure 2, column 4), so hh remains temporally precise even when BB incompletely recovers the underrepresented region.

Quantitative recovery and baselines. Appendix N reports recovery metrics for BB and hh across seeds (precision, recall, interval localization, and noise-covariate split rates), and in Appendix O, we compare TRACE with ℓ\ell-thresholding, censoring thresholding, and ROOT applied to ℓ\ell alone. TRACE recovers the regions where each DGP induces baseline or censoring underrepresentation and is the only method that attributes both mechanisms correctly.

7 Generalizing JTPA Job-Training Effects to a National Target

Applied to the JTPA-to-CPS generalization of Section 1, TRACE reduces the variance objective from V^​(𝟏,𝟎)=81.58\widehat{V}(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{0})=81.58 to V^​(B∗,h∗)=12.68\widehat{V}(B^{*},h^{*})=12.68 (−84.5%-84.5\%), with Rashomon-set objectives between 13.1313.13 and 13.7713.77 and a stable 2/32/3-vote supermajority that trims 46.3%46.3\% of the target and 13.8%13.8\% of the trial. Because h∗h^{*} activates only 98/249,09698/249{,}096 trial person-intervals (0.04%0.04\%, vs. 1,7961{,}796 without R-gating), baseline mismatch, rather than censoring depletion, is the main source of underrepresentation. The 95%95\% CI for the 24-month employment effect is [−10.5,+15.9][-10.5,\,+15.9] percentage points for the original PATE and [−1.9,+8.6][-1.9,\,+8.6] for the refined estimand (−τ^24-\widehat{\tau}_{24}=+0.034=+0.034, SE^=0.027\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}=0.027), a 60.6%60.6\% reduction in width, although the two intervals are for different estimands, the first for the full CPS target and the second for the reliably generalizable subpopulation, which is more credible but less general (Parikh et al., 2025). Because the event in JTPA is first employment (Yt=1Y_{t}=1 while not yet employed; Appendix P.5), all JTPA effects and intervals are reported on the employment scale, i.e., as −τ24-\tau_{24} in the notation of Section 3.1, so that positive values mean training raises the probability of having become employed by month 24.

Localizing JTPA underrepresentation (Figure 3). The BB-tree trims higher socioeconomic status branches common in CPS but rare among the disadvantaged-targeted JTPA enrollees (earnings ≥$8,922\geq\$8{,}922 and married; earnings ≥$14,000\geq\$14{,}000 unmarried; earnings <$8,922<\$8{,}922 with ≥14\geq 14 years of education and married), retaining the typical low-earnings, low-education profile as the reliably generalizable region, which is consistent with the JTPA selection rule (Bloom et al., 1997). Within the (much smaller) censoring-depleted region, the dominant hh-active leaf (earnings <$2,148<\$2{,}148 and ages 2424–4242; n=3,954n=3{,}954) accounts for ∼80%\sim\!80\% of activations and is sharply peaked at t=21t=21 (45/5045/50 leaf interventions), consistent with a late-second-year loss-to-follow-up shock in the window where JTPA’s attrition is documented (Bloom et al., 1997). In short, the trial over-represents the most disadvantaged adults relative to the CPS target (where, baseline why), and late attrition depletes low-earnings young adults (when, temporal why). Details, including sensitivity analyses, are in Appendix P.

8 Discussion

We developed TRACE to find which target subgroups a trial generalizes to, why generalization fails for the others, and when during follow-up precision is lost. The method rests on Theorem 1, by which ℓ⁡(X)\ell(X) and 1/∏j<tπC,ja​(X)1/\prod_{j<t}\pi^{a}_{C,j}(X) are the only channels through which baseline misalignment and differential censoring can inflate variance, and on the coupled interventions (B,h)(B,h) of Theorem 2, which contract each channel separately while the self-normalized objective in (5) penalizes over-trimming. Nesting a parametric DP inside a Rashomon ensemble (Algorithm 3) keeps the search scalable and yields an interpretable four-region partition.

Limitations, future work, and broader impacts. TRACE is diagnostic rather than corrective: it identifies subgroups for whom generalization is unreliable but does not adjust the point estimator τ^T\hat{\tau}_{T}, and the BB-restricted estimand changes the inferential question rather than recovering the original PATE, a trade-off that needs to be described and discussed in any presentation of results. When both mechanisms are large on the same units, how credit is split between them depends on the objective. Likewise, hh flags where and when censoring reduces precision, so its practical use is to guide retention and follow-up in future trials. The point estimate and CI for the BB-restricted PATE are secondary outputs that condition on the selected (B∗,h∗)(B^{*},h^{*}), and inference that accounts for this selection is outside our diagnostic aim. As in the convention for data-defined estimands (Crump et al., 2009; Li et al., 2019; Parikh et al., 2025), we leave such post-selection inference to future work. Extensions include continuous-time survival via counting-process EIFs (Rytgaard et al., 2022; Wen et al., 2025), cross-fit or sample-splitting Rashomon variants that propagate nuisance uncertainty, multi-source generalizations that connect to data fusion (Liu et al., 2025), and corrective methods that use TRACE output for adaptive trial design or targeted oversampling. Reporting which subgroups a trial underrepresents can make evidence-based policy more transparent and equitable. TRACE can, however, be misused if its outputs are read as causal claims about excluded subgroups or if the BB-restricted estimand is conflated with the PATE, and we therefore recommend reporting trimmed-region characteristics with the refined estimand so that the retained population is auditable.

Appendix A Identification and Discussion of Assumptions

We require the following assumptions for identifying PATE.

  1. 1.

    (Consistency). If A=aA=a, then Y¯t=Y¯ta\bar{Y}_{t}=\bar{Y}_{t}^{a} for all t≤Tt\leq T.

  2. 2.

    (Positivity of treatment assignment in the trial). For each treatment aa, if Pr⁡(X=x∣S=1)>0\Pr(X=x\mid S=1)>0, then Pr⁡(A=a∣X=x,S=1)>0\Pr(A=a\mid X=x,S=1)>0.

  3. 3.

    (Exchangeability over treatment assignment in the trial). Yta⟂A|(X,S=1),∀t≤TY_{t}^{a}\perp A\mid(X,S=1),\quad\forall t\leq T.

  4. 4.

    (A1: Censoring positivity in the trial). For each treatment aa, Pr⁡(Ct=0∣C¯t−1=0,Y¯t=1,A=a,X,S=1)>0\Pr(C_{t}=0\mid\bar{C}_{t-1}=0,\,\bar{Y}_{t}=1,\,A=a,\,X,\,S=1)>0 for all t≤T−1t\leq T-1.

  5. 5.

    (A2: Conditional exchangeability in censoring). Y¯t+1⟂Ct|(C¯t−1=0,Y¯t=1,A=a,X,S=1)\underaccent{\bar}{Y}_{t+1}\perp C_{t}\mid(\bar{C}_{t-1}=0,\,\bar{Y}_{t}=1,\,A=a,\,X,\,S=1) for all t≤T−1t\leq T-1.

  6. 6.

    (A3: Conditional exchangeability over SS). For each treatment aa, Yta⟂S|(C¯t−1=0,Y¯t−1=1,A=a,X),∀t≤TY_{t}^{a}\perp S\mid(\bar{C}_{t-1}=0,\;\bar{Y}_{t-1}=1,\;A=a,\;X),\quad\forall t\leq T.

  7. 7.

    (A4: Trial-participation positivity). If Pr⁡(X=x∣S=0)>0\Pr(X=x\mid S=0)>0, then Pr⁡(X=x∣S=1)>0\Pr(X=x\mid S=1)>0.

Discussion of Assumptions.

Consistency, positivity of treatment assignment in the trial, and exchangeability over treatment assignment in the trial are standard conditions assumed in randomized trials and extend to the survival setting. A1 (censoring positivity in the trial) ensures that no subgroup is fully censored at any interval tt, and A2 (conditional exchangeability in censoring) states that, conditional on the history, censoring is missing at random and ignorable. Together with the standard randomization assumptions, A1 and A2 identify the within-trial treatment effect on the survival outcome. A3 (conditional exchangeability over SS) is the generalizability assumption adapted to the time-to-event setting, allowing trial-derived risk-set hazards to be transported to the target conditional on the history; A4 (trial-participation positivity) ensures that every covariate profile prevalent in the target has a corresponding trial counterpart. Under A1–A4, τT​(a)\tau_{T}(a) is identified by an observed-data functional that integrates the within-trial risk-set hazards at each interval, reweighted to the target covariate distribution, as proved below.

By the law of iterated expectations, we first rewrite τt​(a)\tau_{t}(a) as

τt​(a)=𝔼⁡(Yta∣S=0)=𝔼⁡(𝔼⁡(Yta∣X,S=0)|S=0).\tau_{t}(a)=\mathbb{E}(Y_{t}^{a}\mid S=0)=\mathbb{E}\!\left(\,\mathbb{E}(Y_{t}^{a}\mid X,S=0)\,\middle|\,S=0\right).

From A3, we have

𝔼⁡(Yta∣{Yt−1=1,Ct−1=0},X)=\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(Y_{t}^{a}\mid\{Y_{t-1}=1,C_{t-1}=0\},X)= 𝔼⁡(Yta∣{Yt−1=1,Ct−1=0},X,S=0)\displaystyle\;\mathbb{E}(Y_{t}^{a}\mid\{Y_{t-1}=1,C_{t-1}=0\},X,S=0)
=\displaystyle= 𝔼⁡(Yta∣{Yt−1=1,Ct−1=0},X,S=1).\displaystyle\;\mathbb{E}(Y_{t}^{a}\mid\{Y_{t-1}=1,C_{t-1}=0\},X,S=1)\;.

Consequently,

𝔼⁡(Yta∣X)=\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(Y_{t}^{a}\mid X)= 𝔼⁡(Yta∣X,S=0)=𝔼⁡(Yta∣X,S=1).\displaystyle\;\mathbb{E}(Y_{t}^{a}\mid X,S=0)=\mathbb{E}(Y_{t}^{a}\mid X,S=1)\;.

Thus, the PATE can be estimated using the observed data from the trial:

𝔼⁡(Yta∣S=0)=𝔼⁡(𝔼⁡(Yta∣X,S=1)|S=0).\mathbb{E}(Y_{t}^{a}\mid S=0)=\mathbb{E}\!\left(\,\mathbb{E}(Y_{t}^{a}\mid X,S=1)\,\middle|\,S=0\right).

We now focus on the identification of 𝔼⁡(Yta∣X=x,S=1)\mathbb{E}{(}Y^{a}_{t}\mid X=x,S=1). By definition, all individuals are at risk at baseline (i.e., Y0=1Y_{0}=1), and by convention we set C¯−1=0\bar{C}_{-1}=0. From consistency, treatment-assignment positivity, treatment exchangeability, A1, and A2, we have

𝔼⁡(Yta∣X=x,S=1)\displaystyle\quad\;\mathbb{E}(Y_{t}^{a}\mid X=x,S=1)
=𝔼⁡(Yta∣A=a,X=x,S=1)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}{(}Y_{t}^{a}\mid A=a,X=x,S=1) ((Exchangeability over treatment assignment)
=𝔼⁡(Yt∣A=a,X=x,S=1)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}{(}Y_{t}\mid A=a,X=x,S=1) (Consistency)
=𝔼⁡(Yt∣A=a,X=x,S=1,C0=0)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}{(}Y_{t}\mid A=a,X=x,S=1,C_{0}=0) (A2)
=𝔼⁡(Yt∣Y1=1,A=a,X=x,S=1,C0=0)​𝔼​(Y1∣A=a,X=x,S=1,C0=0)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}{(}Y_{t}\mid Y_{1}=1,A=a,X=x,S=1,C_{0}=0)\mathbb{E}{(}Y_{1}\mid A=a,X=x,S=1,C_{0}=0)
=𝔼⁡(Yt∣Y1=1,A=a,X=x,S=1,C1=0,C0=0)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}{(}Y_{t}\mid Y_{1}=1,A=a,X=x,S=1,C_{1}=0,C_{0}=0) (A2)
𝔼⁡(Y1∣A=a,X=x,S=1,C0=0)\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\mathbb{E}{(}Y_{1}\mid A=a,X=x,S=1,C_{0}=0)
=𝔼⁡(Yt∣Y1=1,A=a,X=x,S=1,C1=0)⏟Iterate with previous three steps​𝔼​(Y1∣A=a,X=x,S=1,C0=0)\displaystyle=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}{(}Y_{t}\mid Y_{1}=1,A=a,X=x,S=1,C_{1}=0)}_{\text{{Iterate with previous three steps}}}\mathbb{E}{(}Y_{1}\mid A=a,X=x,S=1,C_{0}=0)
⋮\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\vdots
=𝔼⁡(Yt∣Yt−1=1,A=a,X=x,S=1,Ct−2=0)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}{(}Y_{t}\mid Y_{t-1}=1,A=a,X=x,S=1,C_{t-2}=0)
∏k=1t−1𝔼⁡(Yk∣Yk−1=1,A=a,X=x,S=1,Ck−1=0)\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\prod_{k=1}^{t-1}\mathbb{E}{(}Y_{k}\mid Y_{k-1}=1,A=a,X=x,S=1,C_{k-1}=0)
=𝔼⁡(Yt∣Yt−1=1,A=a,X=x,S=1,Ct−1=0)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}{(}Y_{t}\mid Y_{t-1}=1,A=a,X=x,S=1,C_{t-1}=0) (A2)
∏k=1t−1𝔼⁡(Yk∣Yk−1=1,A=a,X=x,S=1,Ck−1=0)\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\prod_{k=1}^{t-1}\mathbb{E}{(}Y_{k}\mid Y_{k-1}=1,A=a,X=x,S=1,C_{k-1}=0)
=∏k=1t𝔼⁡(Yk∣Yk−1=1,Ck−1=0,X=x,A=a,S=1).\displaystyle=\prod_{k=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}{\!}\left(Y_{k}\mid Y_{k-1}=1,C_{k-1}=0,X=x,A=a,S=1\right)\;. (A3)

Therefore, τt​(a)\tau_{t}(a) can be identified by the observed data functional

ψt​(a)\displaystyle\psi_{t}(a) =𝔼⁡(𝔼⁡(Yta∣X,S=1)|S=0)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left(\,\mathbb{E}(Y_{t}^{a}\mid X,S=1)\,\middle|\,S=0\right)
=𝔼(∏k=1t𝔼(Yk|Yk−1=1,Ck−1=0,X,A=a,S=1)|S=0)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left(\,\prod_{k=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}\!\left(Y_{k}\,\middle|\,Y_{k-1}=1,\;C_{k-1}=0,\;X,\;A=a,\;S=1\right)\,\middle|\,S=0\right)
=𝔼⁡(Pr⁡(S=1)Pr⁡(S=0)⋅Pr⁡(S=0∣X)Pr⁡(S=1∣X)CLOSE\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Bigg(\frac{\Pr(S=1)}{\Pr(S=0)}\cdot\frac{\Pr(S=0\mid X)}{\Pr(S=1\mid X)}
⋅∏k=1t𝔼(Yk|Yk−1=1,Ck−1=0,X,A=a,S=1)|S=1)\displaystyle\hskip 100.00015pt\cdot\prod_{k=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}\!\left(Y_{k}\,\middle|\,Y_{k-1}=1,\;C_{k-1}=0,\;X,\;A=a,\;S=1\right)\,\Bigg|\,S=1\Bigg)
=𝔼⁡(𝟏{S=1}Pr⁡(S=0)⋅Pr⁡(S=0∣X)Pr⁡(S=1∣X)CLOSE\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Bigg(\frac{\mathbf{1}\{S=1\}}{\Pr(S=0)}\cdot\frac{\Pr(S=0\mid X)}{\Pr(S=1\mid X)}
⋅∏k=1t𝔼(Yk|Yk−1=1,Ck−1=0,X,A=a,S=1)).\displaystyle\hskip 100.00015pt\cdot\prod_{k=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}\!\left(Y_{k}\,\middle|\,Y_{k-1}=1,\;C_{k-1}=0,\;X,\;A=a,\;S=1\right)\Bigg)\;.

The PATE at time TT becomes

τT=ψT​(1)−ψT​(0).\tau_{T}=\psi_{T}(1)-\psi_{T}(0)\;.

Appendix B Derivation of EIF

Theorem B.1 (Efficient influence function for τT​(a)\tau_{T}(a)).

Given A1–A4 and standard randomization assumptions, under a nonparametric model on the observed data,

χψT​(a)​(O)\displaystyle\chi_{\psi_{T}(a)}(O) =∑t=1T𝟏​{C¯t−1=0,A=a,S=1}Pr⁡(S=0)​πa​(X)⏟≡Wt−1a​(O)⋅Pr⁡(S=0∣X)Pr⁡(S=1∣X)⏟≡ℓ⁡(X)\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\underbrace{\frac{\mathbf{1}\{\bar{C}_{t-1}=0,\,A=a,\,S=1\}}{\Pr(S=0)\,\pi^{a}(X)}}_{\equiv\,W^{a}_{t-1}(O)}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{\Pr(S=0\mid X)}{\Pr(S=1\mid X)}}_{\equiv\,\ell(X)} (7)
⋅1π¯C,t−1a​(X)⋅[Qta​(X)−Qt−1a​(X)]⏟≡Δ​Qta​(X)+𝟏{S=0}Pr⁡(S=0)​[Q0a​(X)−τT​(a)]\displaystyle\cdot\frac{1}{\bar{\pi}^{a}_{C,t-1}(X)}\cdot\underbrace{\bigl[Q^{a}_{t}(X)-Q^{a}_{t-1}(X)\bigr]}_{\equiv\,\Delta Q^{a}_{t}(X)}\;+\;\frac{\mathbf{1}\{S=0\}}{\Pr(S=0)}\bigl[Q^{a}_{0}(X)-\tau_{T}(a)\bigr]

is the EIF for ψT​(a)=𝔼⁡[YTa∣S=0]\psi_{T}(a)=\mathbb{E}[Y_{T}^{a}\mid S=0], and χτT​(O)=χψT​(1)​(O)−χψT​(0)​(O)\chi_{\tau_{T}}(O)=\chi_{\psi_{T}(1)}(O)-\chi_{\psi_{T}(0)}(O) is the EIF for the contrast.

Proof.

Define the weight

w⁡(X)=𝟏​(S=1)Pr⁡(S=0)⋅Pr⁡(S=0∣X)Pr⁡(S=1∣X).w(X)=\frac{\mathbf{1}(S=1)}{\Pr(S=0)}\cdot\frac{\Pr(S=0\mid X)}{\Pr(S=1\mid X)}\;.

For a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\}, define the treatment probability in the trial as

πa​(X)≡Pr⁡(A=a∣X,S=1),\pi^{a}(X)\equiv\Pr(A=a\mid X,S=1)\;,

the uncensored history up to time kk as

Hka≡(Y¯k=1,C¯k=0,A=a,S=1),H_{k}^{a}\equiv(\bar{Y}_{k}=1,\ \bar{C}_{k}=0,\ A=a,\ S=1)\;,

the probability of being uncensored at time kk given previous history as

πCka​(X)≡Pr⁡(Ck=0∣Yk=1,X,Hk−1a),\pi_{C_{k}}^{a}(X)\equiv\Pr(C_{k}=0\mid Y_{k}=1,\ X,\ H^{a}_{k-1})\;,

and π¯Cka​(X)≡∏j=0k−1πCja​(X)\bar{\pi}^{a}_{C_{k}}(X)\equiv\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}\pi^{a}_{C_{j}}(X). Moreover, let Qta≡YtaQ_{t}^{a}\equiv Y_{t}^{a}, and for k=0,…,t−1k=0,\ldots,t-1, define

Qk−1a​(X)≡𝔼⁡(Qka∣X,Hk−1a)=𝔼⁡(Yta∣X,Hk−1a)=∏j=ktPr⁡(Yj=1∣X,Hj−1a).Q^{a}_{k-1}(X)\equiv\mathbb{E}{\,}\!\bigl(Q_{k}^{a}\mid X,H^{a}_{k-1}\bigr)=\mathbb{E}(Y_{t}^{a}\mid X,H_{k-1}^{a})=\prod_{j=k}^{t}\Pr(Y_{j}=1\mid X,H^{a}_{j-1})\;.

Note that, in the identification formula, we have a series of concatenated conditional expectations. Specifically, the σ\sigma-algebra satisfies

σ⁡(H0a,X)⊂σ⁡(H1a,X)⊂⋯⊂σ⁡(HTa,X).\sigma(H^{a}_{0},X)\subset\sigma(H^{a}_{1},X)\subset\cdots\subset\sigma(H^{a}_{T},X)\;.

Therefore, by the iterated law of conditional expectation, the identification formula can be rewritten as

ψt​(a)≡𝔼⁡(Yta∣S=0)=𝔼⁡[w⁡(X)​Q0a​(X)].\psi_{t}(a)\equiv\mathbb{E}{(}Y_{t}^{a}\mid S=0)=\mathbb{E}{[}w(X)Q^{a}_{0}(X)]\;.

Let

p⁡(S,X,A,C0,(1−C0)×Y1,…,CT−1,(1−CT−1)×YT,θ)p(S,X,A,C_{0},(1-C_{0})\times Y_{1},\ldots,C_{T-1},(1-C_{T-1})\times Y_{T};\theta)

denote a regular parametric submodel of ℳN​P\mathcal{M}_{NP} indexed by θ\theta.

The efficient influence function in ℳN​P\mathcal{M}_{NP} is defined as the unique mean zero, finite variance random variable χψt​(a)​(O)\chi_{\psi_{t}(a)}(O) such that

∂∂θ|θ=0​ψt​(a,θ)=𝔼⁡{χψt​(a)​(O)⋅𝕊⁡(O)},\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\right|_{\theta=0}\psi_{t}(a;\theta)=\mathbb{E}{\!}\left\{\chi_{\psi_{t}(a)}(O)\cdot\mathbb{S}(O)\right\},

where

𝕊⁡(O)=𝕊⁡(S,X,A,C0,(1−C0)×Y1,…,CT−1,(1−CT−1)×YT)\mathbb{S}(O)=\mathbb{S}(S,X,A,C_{0},(1-C_{0})\times Y_{1},\ldots,C_{T-1},(1-C_{T-1})\times Y_{T})

is the score function of the regular parametric submodel at θ=0\theta=0.

By Leibniz rule, for any expectation of function gθ​(O)g_{\theta}(O) under the parametric model p⁡(O,θ)p(O;\theta), we have

dd​θ​𝔼θ​[gθ​(O)]|θ=0=𝔼⁡[∂θgθ​(O)|θ=0]+𝔼⁡[g0​(O)​𝕊​(O)].\left.\frac{d}{d\theta}\,\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\!\left[g_{\theta}(O)\right]\right|_{\theta=0}=\mathbb{E}{\!}\left[\left.\partial_{\theta}g_{\theta}(O)\right|_{\theta=0}\right]+\mathbb{E}{\!}\left[g_{0}(O)\,\mathbb{S}(O)\right].

Now, let gθ​(O)=w⁡(X)​Q0a​(X)g_{\theta}(O)=w(X)Q^{a}_{0}(X), we have

∂θψ⁡(a,θ)|θ=0=𝔼⁡[∂θ(wθ​(X)​Q0,θa​(X))|θ=0]+𝔼⁡[w⁡(X)​Q0a​(X)​𝕊​(O)]=𝔼⁡[w⁡(X)​∂θQ0,θa​(X)|θ=0]+𝔼⁡[Q0a​(X)​∂θwθ​(X)|θ=0]+𝔼⁡[w⁡(X)​Q0a​(X)​𝕊​(O)].\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\quad\left.\partial_{\theta}\psi(a;\theta)\right|_{\theta=0}\\ &=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left.\partial_{\theta}\big(w_{\theta}(X)\,Q^{a}_{0,\theta}(X)\big)\right|_{\theta=0}\right]+\mathbb{E}\!\left[w(X)\,Q^{a}_{0}(X)\,\mathbb{S}(O)\right]\\ &=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left.w(X)\,\partial_{\theta}Q^{a}_{0,\theta}(X)\right|_{\theta=0}\right]+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left.Q^{a}_{0}(X)\,\partial_{\theta}w_{\theta}(X)\right|_{\theta=0}\right]+\mathbb{E}\!\left[w(X)\,Q^{a}_{0}(X)\,\mathbb{S}(O)\right].\end{aligned} (8)

We first focus on the first term, specifically ∂θQ0,θa​(X)|θ=0\partial_{\theta}Q^{a}_{0,\theta}(X)|_{\theta=0}, and introduce the following lemma to help with the iterated conditional expectation.

Lemma 1.

Let XX be a random variable with conditional density pθ​(x∣H=h)p_{\theta}(x\mid H=h) depending smoothly on a scalar parameter θ\theta, and let 𝕊θ​(x∣H)=∂θlog⁡pθ​(x∣H)\mathbb{S}_{\theta}(x\mid H)=\partial_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(x\mid H) denote the conditional score. For any measurable function gg with 𝔼⁡[|g⁡(X)|]<∞\mathbb{E}[|g(X)|]<\infty, we have

∂∂θ|θ=0​𝔼θ​[g⁡(Y)∣H=h]=𝔼⁡[g⁡(Y)​𝕊​(Y∣H)∣H=h],\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\right|_{\theta=0}\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\!\big[g(Y)\mid H=h\big]\;=\;\mathbb{E}\!\big[g(Y)\,\mathbb{S}(Y\mid H)\mid H=h\big],

where 𝕊⁡(Y∣H):=𝕊θ​(Y∣H)|θ=0\mathbb{S}(Y\mid H):=\mathbb{S}_{\theta}(Y\mid H)\big|_{\theta=0}.

Proof of Lemma 1 can be found in Appendix C.

Apply Lemma 1 for Q0,θa​(X)Q^{a}_{0,\theta}(X), we have

Appendix C Proof of Lemma 1

Proof.

Write the conditional expectation as

Eθ​[g⁡(Y)∣H=h]=∫g⁡(y)​pθ​(y∣h)​𝑑y=∫g⁡(y)​pθ​(y,h)​𝑑ypθ​(h).E_{\theta}[g(Y)\mid H=h]=\int g(y)\,p_{\theta}(y\mid h)\,dy=\frac{\int g(y)\,p_{\theta}(y,h)\,dy}{p_{\theta}(h)}.

Differentiating under the integral sign and applying the quotient rule gives

∂θEθ​[g⁡(Y)∣h]=∫g⁡(y)​∂θpθ​(y,h)​𝑑ypθ​(h)−∫g⁡(y)​pθ​(y,h)​𝑑ypθ​(h)2​∂θpθ​(h).\partial_{\theta}E_{\theta}[g(Y)\mid h]=\frac{\int g(y)\,\partial_{\theta}p_{\theta}(y,h)\,dy}{p_{\theta}(h)}-\frac{\int g(y)\,p_{\theta}(y,h)\,dy}{p_{\theta}(h)^{2}}\,\partial_{\theta}p_{\theta}(h).

Since

Sθ​(y,h)=∂θlog⁡pθ​(y,h)=∂θpθ​(y,h)pθ​(y,h),Sθ​(h)=∂θlog⁡pθ​(h)=∂θpθ​(h)pθ​(h),S_{\theta}(y,h)=\partial_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(y,h)=\frac{\partial_{\theta}p_{\theta}(y,h)}{p_{\theta}(y,h)},\qquad S_{\theta}(h)=\partial_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(h)=\frac{\partial_{\theta}p_{\theta}(h)}{p_{\theta}(h)}\,,

we have

∂θpθ​(y,h)=pθ​(y,h)​Sθ​(y,h),∂θpθ​(h)=pθ​(h)​Sθ​(h).\partial_{\theta}p_{\theta}(y,h)=p_{\theta}(y,h)\,S_{\theta}(y,h),\qquad\partial_{\theta}p_{\theta}(h)=p_{\theta}(h)\,S_{\theta}(h).

The derivative becomes

∂θEθ​[g⁡(Y)∣h]=∫g⁡(y)​pθ​(y,h)​Sθ​(y,h)​𝑑ypθ​(h)−∫g⁡(y)​pθ​(y,h)​Sθ​(h)​𝑑ypθ​(h).\partial_{\theta}E_{\theta}[g(Y)\mid h]=\frac{\int g(y)\,p_{\theta}(y,h)\,S_{\theta}(y,h)\,dy}{p_{\theta}(h)}\;-\;\frac{\int g(y)\,p_{\theta}(y,h)\,S_{\theta}(h)\,dy}{p_{\theta}(h)}.

Recognizing the first term as Eθ​[g⁡(Y)​Sθ​(Y,H)∣H=h]E_{\theta}[g(Y)S_{\theta}(Y,H)\mid H=h], the second term as Eθ​[g⁡(Y)​Sθ​(H)∣H=h]E_{\theta}[g(Y)S_{\theta}(H)\mid H=h], and using the identity Sθ​(Y∣H)=Sθ​(Y,H)−Sθ​(H)S_{\theta}(Y\mid H)=S_{\theta}(Y,H)-S_{\theta}(H), we obtain

∂θEθ​[g⁡(Y)∣h]=Eθ​[g⁡(Y)​(Sθ​(Y,H)−Sθ​(H))∣H=h]=Eθ​[g⁡(Y)​Sθ​(Y∣H)∣H=h].\partial_{\theta}E_{\theta}[g(Y)\mid h]=E_{\theta}\!\big[g(Y)(S_{\theta}(Y,H)-S_{\theta}(H))\mid H=h\big]=E_{\theta}\!\big[g(Y)S_{\theta}(Y\mid H)\mid H=h\big].

Evaluating at θ=0\theta=0 yields the result. ∎

Appendix D TMLE Estimator

To construct an estimator that achieves the semiparametric efficiency bound characterized by the EIF, we employ the doubly robust Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimator (TMLE), detailed in Algorithm 1. The TMLE proceeds through a backward recursive targeting procedure that iteratively updates pseudo estimates of the sequential conditional expectations, Qka​(X)Q_{k}^{a}(X). At each step of the backward iteration, the estimator targets the interval-specific component of the EIF. Because these components are sequentially orthogonal, accumulating these targeted updates recursively ensures that the final estimator solves the global EIF equation. Under standard nuisance-rate conditions (op(n−1/4)o_{p}(n^{-1/4}) rates on π^a\hat{\pi}^{a}, π^Ca\hat{\pi}^{a}_{C}, Q^ka\hat{Q}^{a}_{k}, ℓ^\hat{\ell}, and Pr^​(S=0)\hat{\Pr}(S=0), by Donsker class argument or cross-fitting), the resulting TMLE is asymptotically linear and attains the semiparametric efficiency bound.

Appendix E Efficiency Bound

Theorem (Variance decomposition).

Given A1–A4 and standard randomization assumptions, under a nonparametric model on the observed data, the asymptotic variance attaining the semiparametric efficiency bound is

Var{χτT(O)}=∑a∈{0,1}∑t=1T𝔼[(ℓ⁡(X)⏟baseline underrep.)2⋅(∏j<tπC,ja​(X)⏟time-varying underrep.)−2\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}\{\chi_{\tau_{T}}(O)\}=\sum_{a\in\{0,1\}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\biggl[\;\hbox{\pagecolor{red!25}$\displaystyle\bigl(\underbrace{\ell(X)}_{\text{\scriptsize baseline underrep.}}\bigr)^{\!2}$}\cdot\hbox{\pagecolor{red!25}$\displaystyle\biggl(\underbrace{\prod\nolimits_{j<t}\pi^{a}_{C,j}(X)}_{\text{\scriptsize time-varying underrep.}}\biggr)^{\!\!-2}$}
⋅(Wt−1a​(O))2⋅([Qta​(X)]2−[Qt−1a​(X)]2)⏟≤1/[Pr⁡(S=0)2​Pr⁡(A=a∣X,S=1)2]]+𝔼[𝟏{S=0}Pr⁡(S=0)2​(τT​(X)−τT)2⏟≤4/Pr⁡(S=0)2].\displaystyle\cdot\underbrace{\hbox{\pagecolor{green!25}$\displaystyle\bigl(W^{a}_{t-1}(O)\bigr)^{2}\cdot\left(\left[Q^{a}_{t}(X)\right]^{2}-\left[Q^{a}_{t-1}(X)\right]^{2}\right)$}}_{\text{\scriptsize$\leq 1/[\,\Pr(S=0)^{2}\,\Pr(A=a\mid X,S=1)^{2}]$}}\biggr]+\mathbb{E}\!\biggl[\;\underbrace{\hbox{\pagecolor{green!25}$\displaystyle\frac{\mathbf{1}\{S=0\}}{\Pr(S=0)^{2}}\bigl(\tau_{T}(X)-\tau_{T}\bigr)^{2}$}}_{\text{\scriptsize$\leq 4/\Pr(S=0)^{2}$}}\;\biggr]\;.

where Wt−1aW^{a}_{t-1} denotes the trial-at-risk weight, {Qja​(X)}j=0T\{Q^{a}_{j}(X)\}_{j=0}^{T} the iterated conditional survival probabilities, and τT​(X)\tau_{T}(X) the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) at horizon TT.

Proof.

The variance of the TMLE estimator that attains the semiparametric efficiency bound can be estimated using the empirical variance of χτt​(O)\chi_{\tau_{t}}(O), which from Theorem B.1 can be written as

χτt​(O)\displaystyle\chi_{\tau_{t}}(O) =∑k=1t𝟏{S=1} 1{A=1} 1{C¯1k−1=0}Pr⁡(S=0)​π1​(X)​π¯C,k−11​(X)⋅Pr⁡(S=0∣X)Pr⁡(S=1∣X)​[Qk1​(X)−Qk−11​(X)]\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{t}\frac{\mathbf{1}\{S=1\}\,\mathbf{1}\{A=1\}\,\mathbf{1}\{\bar{C}^{1}_{k-1}=0\}}{\Pr(S=0)\,\pi^{1}(X)\,\bar{\pi}^{1}_{C,k-1}(X)}\cdot\frac{\Pr(S=0\mid X)}{\Pr(S=1\mid X)}\,[Q^{1}_{k}(X)-Q^{1}_{k-1}(X)]
−∑k=1t𝟏{S=1} 1{A=0} 1{C¯0k−1=0}Pr⁡(S=0)​π0​(X)​π¯C,k−10​(X)⋅Pr⁡(S=0∣X)Pr⁡(S=1∣X)[Q0k(X)−Q0k−1(X)]\displaystyle-\sum_{k=1}^{t}\frac{\mathbf{1}\{S=1\}\,\mathbf{1}\{A=0\}\,\mathbf{1}\{\bar{C}^{0}_{k-1}=0\}}{\Pr(S=0)\,\pi^{0}(X)\,\bar{\pi}^{0}_{C,k-1}(X)}\cdot\frac{\Pr(S=0\mid X)}{\Pr(S=1\mid X)}\,[Q^{0}_{k}(X)-Q^{0}_{k-1}(X)]
+𝟏{S=0}Pr⁡(S=0)​{[Q01​(X)−Q00​(X)]−τt}.\displaystyle+\frac{\mathbf{1}\{S=0\}}{\Pr(S=0)}\,\bigl\{\,[Q^{1}_{0}(X)-Q^{0}_{0}(X)]-\tau_{t}\,\bigr\}.

Notation aligned with Theorem 1.

We adopt the labels used in the theorem so that the worst-case bounds attach to the correct factors:

  • •

    Baseline underrepresentation (density-ratio) odds

    ℓ⁡(X):=Pr⁡(S=0∣X)Pr⁡(S=1∣X).\ell(X)\;:=\;\frac{\Pr(S=0\mid X)}{\Pr(S=1\mid X)}.
  • •

    Cumulative on-treatment continuation probability (the time-varying underrepresentation factor)

    π¯C,k−1a​(X):=∏j<kπC,ja​(X),a∈{0,1}.\bar{\pi}^{a}_{C,k-1}(X)\;:=\;\prod_{j<k}\pi^{a}_{C,j}(X),\qquad a\in\{0,1\}.
  • •

    Trial-at-risk weight

    Wk−1a​(O):=𝟏{S=1} 1{A=a} 1{C¯ak−1=0}Pr⁡(S=0)​πa​(X).W^{a}_{k-1}(O)\;:=\;\frac{\mathbf{1}\{S=1\}\,\mathbf{1}\{A=a\}\,\mathbf{1}\{\bar{C}^{a}_{k-1}=0\}}{\Pr(S=0)\,\pi^{a}(X)}.
  • •

    Martingale increment Δka:=Qka​(X)−Qk−1a​(X)\Delta_{k}^{a}:=Q^{a}_{k}(X)-Q^{a}_{k-1}(X), and CATE at horizon tt, τt​(X):=Q01​(X)−Q00​(X)\tau_{t}(X):=Q^{1}_{0}(X)-Q^{0}_{0}(X).

The EIF in factorized form.

Substituting the above factors into the EIF and using τt​(X)=Q01​(X)−Q00​(X)\tau_{t}(X)=Q^{1}_{0}(X)-Q^{0}_{0}(X),

χτt​(O)\displaystyle\chi_{\tau_{t}}(O) =∑k=1tℓ⁡(X)​[π¯C,k−11​(X)]−1​Wk−11​(O)​Δk1\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{t}\ell(X)\,\bigl[\bar{\pi}^{1}_{C,k-1}(X)\bigr]^{-1}\,W^{1}_{k-1}(O)\,\Delta_{k}^{1}
−∑k=1tℓ(X)[π¯0C,k−1(X)]−1W0k−1(O)Δk0\displaystyle-\sum_{k=1}^{t}\ell(X)\,\bigl[\bar{\pi}^{0}_{C,k-1}(X)\bigr]^{-1}\,W^{0}_{k-1}(O)\,\Delta_{k}^{0}
+𝟏{S=0}Pr⁡(S=0)​{τt​(X)−τt}.\displaystyle+\frac{\mathbf{1}\{S=0\}}{\Pr(S=0)}\bigl\{\tau_{t}(X)-\tau_{t}\bigr\}.

Define the per-period summands

χψt,ka:=ℓ⁡(X)​[π¯C,k−1a​(X)]−1​Wk−1a​(O)​Δka,a∈{0,1}.\chi^{a}_{\psi_{t},k}\;:=\;\ell(X)\,\bigl[\bar{\pi}^{a}_{C,k-1}(X)\bigr]^{-1}\,W^{a}_{k-1}(O)\,\Delta_{k}^{a},\qquad a\in\{0,1\}.

Orthogonality across tangent spaces and across kk.

The three pieces of χτt​(O)\chi_{\tau_{t}}(O) live in orthogonal tangent spaces indexed by 𝟏​{S=1,A=1}\mathbf{1}\{S=1,A=1\}, 𝟏​{S=1,A=0}\mathbf{1}\{S=1,A=0\}, and 𝟏{S=0}\mathbf{1}\{S=0\}, so cross-component covariances vanish. The hi,j/2h_{i,j}/2 exponent.

Aside from BB, the variance in Theorem 2 differs from the original Var​{χτT​(O)}\mathrm{Var}\{\chi_{\tau_{T}}(O)\} from Theorem 1 in the exponent of the IPCW’s. Setting hi,j=1h_{i,j}=1 induces two simultaneous changes from 𝒫\mathcal{P} to the hypothetical 𝒫i∗\mathcal{P}^{*}_{i}: (i) the IPCW πC,ja​(X)−1\pi^{a}_{C,j}(X)^{-1} collapses to 11, since nobody is censored at interval jj; and (ii) the effective sample at interval jj grows by a factor of πC,ja​(X)−1\pi^{a}_{C,j}(X)^{-1}, since units that would be censored under 𝒫\mathcal{P} at time jj are now retained. Naively zeroing the IPCW exponent (1/π→11/\pi\to 1) captures (i) but not (ii). It removes the censoring weight without reweighting for the under-observed units, overcorrecting for the censoring inflation. The exponent 1−hi,j/21-h_{i,j}/2 is the unique scalar correction that scales the observed sample up to its 𝒫i∗\mathcal{P}^{*}_{i} counterpart.

Appendix H Derivation of the Empirical Objective V^​(B,h)\widehat{V}(B,h)

The empirical objective in (5) arises from the standard plug-in recipe applied to V⁡(B,h)V(B,h) of Theorem 2: sample averages in place of expectations, fitted nuisances in place of population nuisances. The only remaining choice concerns the factor 1/pB21/p_{B}^{2} that multiplies both summands of V⁡(B,h)V(B,h), since pBp_{B} admits two candidate Hájek surrogates, one from the trial side and one from the target. Pairing each summand with its own surrogate, rather than imposing a shared one, gives the estimator a finite-sample property we explain below. We proceed in three steps: factor 1/pB21/p_{B}^{2} out of V⁡(B,h)V(B,h) (via Appendix G), identify the two surrogates (via Appendices A and F), and verify consistency under the regularity conditions stated next.

Assumption B (regularity for asymptotic linearity).

The consistency result below requires the standard semiparametric regularity conditions used to establish asymptotic linearity of the TMLE in Appendix D.

  1. B1.

    (Cross-fitting / Donsker.) The nuisance functions ℓ\ell, πa\pi^{a}, πC,ka\pi^{a}_{C,k}, QkaQ^{a}_{k} are estimated on cross-fitted folds, or alternatively, they lie in Donsker classes (Chernozhukov et al., 2018; van der Laan and Rose, 2018).

  2. B2.

    (Rates.) ∥ℓ^−ℓ∥2=op(n−1/4)\|\hat{\ell}-\ell\|_{2}=o_{p}(n^{-1/4}), and analogous op(n−1/4)o_{p}(n^{-1/4}) rates hold for π^a\hat{\pi}^{a}, π^C,ka\hat{\pi}^{a}_{C,k}, and Q^ka\hat{Q}^{a}_{k}.

  3. B3.

    (Positivity.) ℓ⁡(X)\ell(X) and π¯C,T−1a​(X)\bar{\pi}^{a}_{C,T-1}(X) are bounded away from 00 and ∞\infty on {X:B⁡(X)=1}\{X:B(X)=1\}.

  4. B4.

    (Integrability.) All nuisance functions are in L2​(P)L^{2}(P).

(B1) and (B2) are the rate conditions that drive the empirical-process remainder and the cross-product bias to op(n−1/2)o_{p}(n^{-1/2}); (B3) keeps the Hájek denominators bounded away from zero on the kept population; (B4) supplies the L2L^{2} moment needed for the LLN. Together they reproduce the conditions under which the TMLE in Appendix D attains the semiparametric efficiency bound, restricted to the BB-kept subpopulation.

Factoring 1/pB21/p_{B}^{2} out of V⁡(B,h)V(B,h).

Step 4 of the proof of Theorem 2 in Appendix G shows that the trial integrand at (X=x,A=a,S=1)(X{=}x,\,A{=}a,\,S{=}1) factors as (B⁡(x)​ℓ​(x))2​πa​(x)−2​pB−2(B(x)\ell(x))^{2}\,\pi^{a}(x)^{-2}\,p_{B}^{-2} times the censoring-and-survival piece. The target block of (3) already carries 1/pB21/p_{B}^{2} explicitly, so we may pull the factor outside both summands at once:

V⁡(B,h)=1pB2​{Mtrl​(B,h)+Mtgt​(B)},V(B,h)\;=\;\frac{1}{p_{B}^{2}}\,\bigl\{\,M_{\text{trl}}(B,h)\,+\,M_{\text{tgt}}(B)\,\bigr\}, (11)

with Mtrl(B,h)=𝔼[𝟏{S=1}B(X)Ψ∘(O;h)]M_{\text{trl}}(B,h)=\mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\mathbf{1}\{S{=}1\}\,B(X)\,\Psi^{\circ}(O;h)\bigr], Mtgt(B)=𝔼[𝟏{S=0}B(X)(τT(X)−τT(B))2]M_{\text{tgt}}(B)=\mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\mathbf{1}\{S{=}0\}\,B(X)\,(\tau_{T}(X)-\tau_{T}(B))^{2}\bigr], and per-unit kernel

Ψ∘​(Oi,hi)=ℓ​(Xi)2​∑a,t𝟏​{Ai=a,C¯i,t−1=0}πa​(Xi)2​∏j<tπC,ja​(Xi)2​(1−hi,j/2)​([Qta​(Xi)]2−[Qt−1a​(Xi)]2).\Psi^{\circ}(O_{i};h_{i})\;=\;\ell(X_{i})^{2}\sum_{a,t}\frac{\mathbf{1}\{A_{i}{=}a,\,\bar{C}_{i,t-1}{=}0\}}{\pi^{a}(X_{i})^{2}\,\prod_{j<t}\pi^{a}_{C,j}(X_{i})^{2(1-h_{i,j}/2)}}\bigl([Q^{a}_{t}(X_{i})]^{2}-[Q^{a}_{t-1}(X_{i})]^{2}\bigr).

Two surrogates for pBp_{B}.

Apply the substitutions ℓ⁡(X)↦B⁡(X)​ℓ​(X)\ell(X)\mapsto B(X)\ell(X) and Pr⁡(S=0)↦pB\Pr(S{=}0)\mapsto p_{B} from the proof of Theorem F.1 (Appendix F) to the identification identity 𝔼[𝟏{S=1}ℓ(X)]=Pr(S=0)\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}\{S{=}1\}\ell(X)]=\Pr(S{=}0) of Appendix A. The result is the chain

𝔼[𝟏{S=1}ℓ(X)B(X)]=𝔼X[B(X)Pr(S=0∣X)]=𝔼[𝟏{S=0}B(X)]=pB,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathbf{1}\{S{=}1\}\,\ell(X)\,B(X)\bigr]\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{X}\!\bigl[B(X)\,\Pr(S{=}0\mid X)\bigr]\;=\;\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathbf{1}\{S{=}0\}\,B(X)\bigr]\;=\;p_{B},

and either end yields an estimator of pBp_{B}. The trial-side Hájek average p^Btrl=n−1∑i:Si=1ℓ^(Xi)B(Xi)\hat{p}_{B}^{\text{trl}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i:S_{i}=1}\hat{\ell}(X_{i})\,B(X_{i}) is consistent for pBp_{B} once ℓ^→pℓ\hat{\ell}\to_{p}\ell, which holds at the (B1)–(B2) rate; the target-side sample mean p^Btgt=n−1∑i:Si=0B(Xi)\hat{p}_{B}^{\text{tgt}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i:S_{i}=0}B(X_{i}) is consistent by the LLN on bounded i.i.d. summands.

Pairing each block with its own surrogate.

Replacing 1/pB21/p_{B}^{2} in (11) by either 1/(p^Btrl)21/(\hat{p}_{B}^{\text{trl}})^{2} or 1/(p^Btgt)21/(\hat{p}_{B}^{\text{tgt}})^{2} throughout still yields a consistent estimator, so the choice of pairing does not change the asymptotics. It changes finite-sample behaviour. Trimming a trial unit shrinks p^Btrl\hat{p}_{B}^{\text{trl}} but leaves p^Btgt\hat{p}_{B}^{\text{tgt}} untouched, and trimming a target unit does the opposite. Pairing each block with its native surrogate therefore gives each side a self-regulating denominator that changes only with its own trims, and this separation allows the trim threshold of Theorem I.1 to factor into an independent trial-side condition and an independent target-side condition. A shared denominator would couple the two sides and break the factorization.

The estimator.

Plug the empirical analogs of MtrlM_{\text{trl}} and MtgtM_{\text{tgt}} into (11), replace the population nuisances inside Ψ∘\Psi^{\circ} by their fitted counterparts (write Ψ\Psi for the result), and pair each appearance of 1/pB21/p_{B}^{2} with its native surrogate. This gives

V^(B,h)=1n​(p^Btrl)2∑i:Si=1B(Xi)Ψ(Oi;hi)+1n​(p^Btgt)2∑i:Si=0B(Xi)(τ^(Xi)−τ^T(B))2,\widehat{V}(B,h)\;=\;\frac{1}{n\,(\hat{p}_{B}^{\text{trl}})^{2}}\!\!\sum_{i:S_{i}=1}\!\!B(X_{i})\,\Psi(O_{i};h_{i})\;+\;\frac{1}{n\,(\hat{p}_{B}^{\text{tgt}})^{2}}\!\!\sum_{i:S_{i}=0}\!\!B(X_{i})\,(\hat{\tau}(X_{i})-\hat{\tau}_{T}(B))^{2},

which is (5).

Proposition 1 (Mixed-Hájek consistency).

Under A1–A4, B1–B4, and pB>0p_{B}>0, V^(B,h)→pV(B,h)\widehat{V}(B,h)\to_{p}V(B,h).

Proof.

Both blocks of V^​(B,h)\widehat{V}(B,h) take the form N∙/D∙2N_{\bullet}/D_{\bullet}^{2}, with N∙N_{\bullet} a sample mean and D∙D_{\bullet} a Hájek surrogate. The numerators converge to MtrlM_{\text{trl}} and MtgtM_{\text{tgt}} by the same nuisance-control argument that established asymptotic linearity of the TMLE in Appendix D: (B4) supplies the L2L^{2} moment needed for the LLN, (B1) drives the empirical-process remainder to op(n−1/2)o_{p}(n^{-1/2}) via cross-fitting or a Donsker condition, and (B2)’s op(n−1/4)o_{p}(n^{-1/4}) rates push the cross-product bias from ℓ^,π^a,π^C,ja,Q^ka\hat{\ell},\hat{\pi}^{a},\hat{\pi}^{a}_{C,j},\hat{Q}^{a}_{k} to the same order. The denominators converge to pBp_{B} by the calculation above, and (B3) keeps pB2p_{B}^{2} bounded away from zero. Continuous mapping applied to g⁡(N,D2)=N/D2g(N,D^{2})=N/D^{2} then gives V^(B,h)→p(Mtrl+Mtgt)/pB2\widehat{V}(B,h)\to_{p}(M_{\text{trl}}+M_{\text{tgt}})/p_{B}^{2}, which equals V⁡(B,h)V(B,h) by (11). ∎
