For any kept individual jj, exactly one block of V^\widehat{V} changes when B⁡(Xj)B(X_{j}) flips to 00, so the marginal trim is variance-reducing iff the above one-sided condition holds:

{ℓ^​(Xj)​Ψ​(Oj,hj∗)> 2​r¯kepttrl​(B)+op​(1)if ​Sj=1,(τ^​(Xj)−τ^T​(B))2> 2​(τ−τ^T)2¯kept​(B)+op​(1)if ​Sj=0.\begin{cases}\hat{\ell}(X_{j})\,\Psi(O_{j};h^{*}_{j})\;>\;2\,\bar{r}^{\text{trl}}_{\text{kept}}(B)\;+\;o_{p}(1)&\text{if }S_{j}=1,\\[4.0pt] \bigl(\hat{\tau}(X_{j})-\hat{\tau}_{T}(B)\bigr)^{2}\;>\;2\,\overline{(\tau-\hat{\tau}_{T})^{2}}_{\text{kept}}(B)\;+\;o_{p}(1)&\text{if }S_{j}=0.\end{cases}

For trial jj, Ψ⁡(Oj,hj∗)\Psi(O_{j};h^{*}_{j}) is undefined off the trial sample so the second LHS is identically 00; for target jj, the trial-side leverage Ψ\Psi depends on observed (Aj,C¯j,Y¯j)(A_{j},\bar{C}_{j},\bar{Y}_{j}) and is similarly identically 00 off the target. Each case therefore matches (12) of Theorem I.1 with the LHS reduced to its surviving term and the RHS reduced to twice the kept-mean of the changing block. ∎

Appendix J Parametric Dynamic Programming for the Inner Optimization

This appendix derives the parametric DP referenced in Section 5.1 and proves Theorem 3 below. Fix a baseline trim BB. From (2), the inner problem is

h∗​(B)=arg⁡minh∈{0,1}n1×T​V^​(B,h)+λh​‖h‖1.h^{*}(B)\;=\;\arg\min_{h\in\{0,1\}^{n_{1}\times T}}\;\widehat{V}(B,h)\;+\;\lambda_{h}\,\|h\|_{1}. (16)

Despite involving n1⋅Tn_{1}\cdot T binary variables, (16) reduces to a precomputable per-individual table queried at 𝒪⁡(n1​T)\mathcal{O}(n_{1}T) cost per outer-loop candidate BB. We establish this in five steps: (i) decouple V^​(B,h)\widehat{V}(B,h) across trial individuals; (ii) collapse the treatment-arm sum onto the observed arm; (iii) rewrite the multiplicative censoring product as an exponential of an additive state; (iv) prove that the per-individual minimum reduces to a (T+1)(T{+}1)-piece affine envelope (Lemma 2); (v) compute the envelope slopes via a budget-augmented Bellman recursion (Proposition 2), with a discretization plus exact-recompute correction that yields exact slopes from near-optimal policies.

J.1 Per-individual decoupling

Let ℐ1:={i:Si=1}\mathcal{I}_{1}:=\{i:S_{i}=1\} denote the trial sample. Inspecting the trial block of (5) term-by-term, ∑i:Si=1\sum_{i:S_{i}=1} is a sum of contributions each depending on a single index ii, so

V^(B,h)=∑i∈ℐ1Vitrl​(B,hi)⏟trial-side, depends on ​h+1n​(p^Btgt)2∑i:Si=0B(Xi)(τ^(Xi)−τ^T(B))2⏟target-side, no ​h​ dependence,\widehat{V}(B,h)\;=\;\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}V_{i}^{\text{trl}}(B,h_{i})}_{\text{trial-side, depends on }h}\;+\;\underbrace{\frac{1}{n\,(\hat{p}_{B}^{\text{tgt}})^{2}}\sum_{i:\,S_{i}=0}B(X_{i})\bigl(\hat{\tau}(X_{i})-\hat{\tau}_{T}(B)\bigr)^{2}}_{\text{target-side, no }h\text{ dependence}},

where hi=(hi,1,…,hi,T)∈{0,1}Th_{i}=(h_{i,1},\ldots,h_{i,T})\in\{0,1\}^{T} collects unit ii’s interventions and the per-individual trial contribution is

Vitrl​(B,hi)\displaystyle V_{i}^{\text{trl}}(B,h_{i}) =1n​(p^Btrl)2∑a∈{0,1}∑t=1TB(Xi)ℓ^(Xi)2 1{C¯i,t−1=0}\displaystyle=\;\frac{1}{n\,(\hat{p}_{B}^{\text{trl}})^{2}}\sum_{a\in\{0,1\}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}B(X_{i})\,\hat{\ell}(X_{i})^{2}\,\mathbf{1}\{\bar{C}_{i,t-1}=0\} (17)
⋅∏j<tπ^C,ja​(Xi)−2​(1−hi,j/2)​Δ​Q^ta​(Xi)2π^a​(Xi)2,\displaystyle\cdot\,\prod_{j<t}\hat{\pi}^{a}_{C,j}(X_{i})^{-2(1-h_{i,j}/2)}\,\frac{\Delta\hat{Q}_{t}^{a}(X_{i})^{2}}{\hat{\pi}^{a}(X_{i})^{2}},

with π^a​(Xi)=Pr⁡(Ai=a∣Xi,Si=1)\hat{\pi}^{a}(X_{i})=\Pr(A_{i}=a\mid X_{i},S_{i}=1) and Δ​Q^ta​(Xi)2:=[Q^ta​(Xi)]2−[Q^t−1a​(Xi)]2\Delta\hat{Q}_{t}^{a}(X_{i})^{2}:=[\hat{Q}_{t}^{a}(X_{i})]^{2}-[\hat{Q}_{t-1}^{a}(X_{i})]^{2}. The penalty also separates, λh​‖h‖1=∑i∈ℐ1λh​‖hi‖1\lambda_{h}\|h\|_{1}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}\lambda_{h}\|h_{i}\|_{1}, and the target-side term is constant in hh. Hence

h∗​(B)=(hi∗​(B))i∈ℐ1,hi∗​(B)=arg⁡minhi∈{0,1}T​[Vitrl​(B,hi)+λh​‖hi‖1],h^{*}(B)\;=\;\bigl(h_{i}^{*}(B)\bigr)_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{1}},\qquad h_{i}^{*}(B)\;=\;\arg\min_{h_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{T}}\bigl[V_{i}^{\text{trl}}(B,h_{i})+\lambda_{h}\,\|h_{i}\|_{1}\bigr],

and we restrict attention to a single individual ii for the remainder.

J.2 Arm-sum collapse to the observed arm

Equation (17) sums over a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\}, but only one arm is observed per individual. The factor 𝟏{C¯i,t−1=0}\mathbf{1}\{\bar{C}_{i,t-1}=0\} indicates that ii has not been censored by time t−1t{-}1; censoring, like the survival outcome, is observed only under the assigned arm AiA_{i}. For the counterfactual arm a≠Aia\neq A_{i}, C¯i,t−1\bar{C}_{i,t-1} is undefined, and by the standard IPW convention we set 𝟏{C¯i,t−1=0}=𝟏{Ai=a}⋅𝟏{C¯i,t−1=0∣Ai=a}\mathbf{1}\{\bar{C}_{i,t-1}=0\}=\mathbf{1}\{A_{i}=a\}\cdot\mathbf{1}\{\bar{C}_{i,t-1}=0\mid A_{i}=a\}. Only the term a=Aia=A_{i} survives, and

Vitrl​(B,hi)\displaystyle V_{i}^{\text{trl}}(B,h_{i}) =B⁡(Xi)​ℓ^​(Xi)2n​(p^Btrl)2​π^Ai​(Xi)2\displaystyle=\;\frac{B(X_{i})\,\hat{\ell}(X_{i})^{2}}{n\,(\hat{p}_{B}^{\text{trl}})^{2}\,\hat{\pi}^{A_{i}}(X_{i})^{2}} (18)
⋅∑t=1T[∏j<tπ^AiC,j(Xi)−2​(1−hi,j/2)] 1{C¯i,t−1=0}ΔQ^tAi(Xi)2.\displaystyle\cdot\sum_{t=1}^{T}\biggl[\prod_{j<t}\hat{\pi}^{A_{i}}_{C,j}(X_{i})^{-2(1-h_{i,j}/2)}\biggr]\,\mathbf{1}\{\bar{C}_{i,t-1}=0\}\,\Delta\hat{Q}_{t}^{A_{i}}(X_{i})^{2}.

This is a sum over TT time points only, with all quantities indexed by the observed arm AiA_{i}.

J.3 Censoring product as an exponential of an additive state

Take the logarithm of the censoring product in (18),

log∏j<tπ^C,jAi(Xi)−2​(1−hi,j/2)=∑j<t(−2logπ^C,jAi(Xi))(1−hi,j/2),\log\prod_{j<t}\hat{\pi}^{A_{i}}_{C,j}(X_{i})^{-2(1-h_{i,j}/2)}\;=\;\sum_{j<t}\bigl(-2\log\hat{\pi}^{A_{i}}_{C,j}(X_{i})\bigr)\bigl(1-h_{i,j}/2\bigr),

and define the per-individual increment δi,j:=−2​log⁡π^C,jAi​(Xi)≥0\delta_{i,j}:=-2\log\hat{\pi}^{A_{i}}_{C,j}(X_{i})\geq 0 (non-negativity follows from π^C,jAi​(Xi)∈(0,1]\hat{\pi}^{A_{i}}_{C,j}(X_{i})\in(0,1]). Then

∏j<tπ^C,jAi​(Xi)−2​(1−hi,j/2)=exp⁡(∑j<tδi,j​(1−hi,j/2)).\prod_{j<t}\hat{\pi}^{A_{i}}_{C,j}(X_{i})^{-2(1-h_{i,j}/2)}\;=\;\exp\!\Bigl(\,\sum_{j<t}\delta_{i,j}(1-h_{i,j}/2)\Bigr). (19)

Define the cumulative state si,t​(hi):=∑j<tδi,j​(1−hi,j/2)s_{i,t}(h_{i}):=\sum_{j<t}\delta_{i,j}(1-h_{i,j}/2), with si,1​(hi)=0s_{i,1}(h_{i})=0 and recursive update

si,t+1​(hi)=si,t​(hi)+δi,t​(1−hi,t/2).s_{i,t+1}(h_{i})\;=\;s_{i,t}(h_{i})+\delta_{i,t}\bigl(1-h_{i,t}/2\bigr). (20)

The state si,ts_{i,t} is the transition variable of the DP in Section J.6.

J.4 Per-individual reduction

Substituting (19) into (18) and introducing the hh-free constants

Ci,t\displaystyle C_{i,t} :=ℓ^(Xi)2 1{C¯i,t−1=0}ΔQ^tAi(Xi)2π^Ai​(Xi)2,\displaystyle\;:=\;\frac{\hat{\ell}(X_{i})^{2}\,\mathbf{1}\{\bar{C}_{i,t-1}=0\}\,\Delta\hat{Q}_{t}^{A_{i}}(X_{i})^{2}}{\hat{\pi}^{A_{i}}(X_{i})^{2}}, (21)
αi​(B)\displaystyle\alpha_{i}(B) :=B⁡(Xi)n​(p^Btrl)2,\displaystyle\;:=\;\frac{B(X_{i})}{n\,(\hat{p}_{B}^{\text{trl}})^{2}}, (22)

yields the per-individual factorization

Vitrl​(B,hi)=αi​(B)​∑t=1TCi,t​exp⁡(si,t​(hi)).V_{i}^{\text{trl}}(B,h_{i})\;=\;\alpha_{i}(B)\sum_{t=1}^{T}C_{i,t}\,\exp\!\bigl(s_{i,t}(h_{i})\bigr). (23)

The constants Ci,tC_{i,t} and δi,t\delta_{i,t} depend only on the nuisance fits and the observed data; αi​(B)\alpha_{i}(B) depends on BB but not on hh. Writing ℒi​(B,hi):=Vitrl​(B,hi)+λh​‖hi‖1\mathcal{L}_{i}(B,h_{i}):=V_{i}^{\text{trl}}(B,h_{i})+\lambda_{h}\|h_{i}\|_{1} gives

ℒi​(B,hi)=αi​(B)​∑t=1TCi,t​exp⁡(si,t​(hi))+λh​∑t=1Thi,t.\mathcal{L}_{i}(B,h_{i})\;=\;\alpha_{i}(B)\sum_{t=1}^{T}C_{i,t}\,\exp\!\bigl(s_{i,t}(h_{i})\bigr)\;+\;\lambda_{h}\sum_{t=1}^{T}h_{i,t}. (24)

Structural observation.

For any fixed hi∈{0,1}Th_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{T}, ℒi​(B,hi)=m⁡(hi)⋅αi​(B)+n⁡(hi)⋅λh\mathcal{L}_{i}(B,h_{i})=m(h_{i})\cdot\alpha_{i}(B)+n(h_{i})\cdot\lambda_{h} is affine in (αi,λh)(\alpha_{i},\lambda_{h}), with slope m⁡(hi):=∑tCi,t​exp⁡(si,t​(hi))m(h_{i}):=\sum_{t}C_{i,t}\exp(s_{i,t}(h_{i})) and intercept coefficient n⁡(hi):=‖hi‖1n(h_{i}):=\|h_{i}\|_{1}. The minimum over {0,1}T\{0,1\}^{T} is therefore a lower envelope of 2T2^{T} affine functions on the (αi,λh)(\alpha_{i},\lambda_{h}) plane. The second coefficient n⁡(hi)=‖hi‖1n(h_{i})=\|h_{i}\|_{1} takes only T+1T{+}1 distinct integer values {0,1,…,T}\{0,1,\ldots,T\}, and we exploit this in Lemma 2.

J.5 Budget sufficiency

Lemma 2 (Budget sufficiency).

For each i∈ℐ1i\in\mathcal{I}_{1},

minhi∈{0,1}T⁡ℒi​(B,hi)=minj∈{0,1,…,T}⁡[αi​(B)⋅fi,j+λh⋅j],\min_{h_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{T}}\!\mathcal{L}_{i}(B,h_{i})\;=\;\min_{j\in\{0,1,\ldots,T\}}\!\bigl[\alpha_{i}(B)\cdot f_{i,j}\,+\,\lambda_{h}\cdot j\bigr], (25)

where the slope at budget level jj is

fi,j:=min⁡∑t=1Thi∈{0,1}T‖hi‖1=j⁡Ci,t​exp⁡(si,t​(hi)).f_{i,j}\;:=\;\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}h_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{T}\\ \|h_{i}\|_{1}=j\end{subarray}}\;\sum_{t=1}^{T}C_{i,t}\,\exp\!\bigl(s_{i,t}(h_{i})\bigr). (26)
Proof.

Partition {0,1}T=⨆j=0Tℋj\{0,1\}^{T}=\bigsqcup_{j=0}^{T}\mathcal{H}_{j} by ℋj:={hi:‖hi‖1=j}\mathcal{H}_{j}:=\{h_{i}:\|h_{i}\|_{1}=j\}. For any hi∈ℋjh_{i}\in\mathcal{H}_{j},

ℒi​(B,hi)=αi​(B)​∑tCi,t​exp⁡(si,t​(hi))+λh⋅j,\mathcal{L}_{i}(B,h_{i})\;=\;\alpha_{i}(B)\sum_{t}C_{i,t}\,\exp\!\bigl(s_{i,t}(h_{i})\bigr)\;+\;\lambda_{h}\cdot j,

with λh⋅j\lambda_{h}\cdot j constant on ℋj\mathcal{H}_{j}. Hence minhi∈ℋj⁡ℒi​(B,hi)=αi​(B)⋅fi,j+λh⋅j\min_{h_{i}\in\mathcal{H}_{j}}\mathcal{L}_{i}(B,h_{i})=\alpha_{i}(B)\cdot f_{i,j}+\lambda_{h}\cdot j, and minimizing across partition classes yields (25). ∎

The right-hand side of (25) is a lower envelope of T+1T{+}1 affine functions of αi​(B)\alpha_{i}(B), with slopes fi,0,…,fi,Tf_{i,0},\ldots,f_{i,T} and intercepts 0,λh,…,T​λh0,\lambda_{h},\ldots,T\lambda_{h}. The slopes are monotone non-increasing, fi,0≥fi,1≥⋯≥fi,Tf_{i,0}\geq f_{i,1}\geq\cdots\geq f_{i,T}: any hi∈ℋj−1h_{i}\in\mathcal{H}_{j-1} admits a coordinate flip 0→10\to 1 to land in ℋj\mathcal{H}_{j}, and adding interventions can only decrease si,ts_{i,t} (since δi,t​(1−hi,t/2)≤δi,t\delta_{i,t}(1-h_{i,t}/2)\leq\delta_{i,t}), hence decrease ∑tCi,t​exp⁡(si,t)\sum_{t}C_{i,t}\exp(s_{i,t}).

The slopes {fi,j}j=0T\{f_{i,j}\}_{j=0}^{T} depend only on (Ci,⋅,δi,⋅)(C_{i,\cdot},\delta_{i,\cdot}), which are functions of nuisance fits and observed data; they are independent of BB and λh\lambda_{h}. This is the decoupling property of Section 4.2: the slopes can be precomputed once per individual and reused for every candidate BB and every choice of penalty λh\lambda_{h}.

J.6 Budget-augmented Bellman recursion

Equation (26) defines fi,jf_{i,j} as a minimum of (Tj)\binom{T}{j} values; direct enumeration is infeasible for moderate TT. We exploit the additive state structure of si,ts_{i,t} via dynamic programming. Fix ii and drop the subscript: write Ct,δt,ht,stC_{t},\delta_{t},h_{t},s_{t}. For k∈{1,…,T+1}k\in\{1,\ldots,T+1\}, s∈ℝ≥0s\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}, and j∈{0,1,…,T}j\in\{0,1,\ldots,T\}, define the partial value function

Uk​(s,j):=min⁡∑t=kT(hk,…,hT)∈{0,1}T−k+1∑t=kTht=j⁡Ct​exp⁡(st),U_{k}(s,j)\;:=\;\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}(h_{k},\ldots,h_{T})\in\{0,1\}^{T-k+1}\\ \sum_{t=k}^{T}h_{t}=j\end{subarray}}\;\sum_{t=k}^{T}C_{t}\,\exp(s_{t}), (27)

where the state evolves from sk=ss_{k}=s via st+1=st+δt​(1−ht/2)s_{t+1}=s_{t}+\delta_{t}(1-h_{t}/2) for t=k,…,T−1t=k,\ldots,T-1, with the convention ∑t=T+1T=0\sum_{t=T+1}^{T}=0.

Proposition 2 (Bellman recursion for UkU_{k}).

The value function (27) satisfies the recursion

Uk(s,j)=min{\displaystyle U_{k}(s,j)\;=\;\min\!\Bigl\{ Ck​es+Uk+1​(s+δk,j)⏟action ​hk=0,\displaystyle\underbrace{C_{k}\,e^{s}+U_{k+1}(s+\delta_{k},\,j)}_{\text{action }h_{k}=0},\; (28)
Ck​es+Uk+1​(s+δk/2,j−1)⏟action ​hk=1,j≥1},\displaystyle\underbrace{C_{k}\,e^{s}+U_{k+1}(s+\delta_{k}/2,\,j-1)}_{\text{action }h_{k}=1,\,j\geq 1}\,\Bigr\},

with the hk=1h_{k}=1 branch replaced by +∞+\infty when j=0j=0, and terminal condition UT+1​(s,0)=0U_{T+1}(s,0)=0, UT+1​(s,j)=+∞U_{T+1}(s,j)=+\infty for j≥1j\geq 1. The slopes of Lemma 2 are recovered by fi,j=U1​(0,j)f_{i,j}=U_{1}(0,j).

Proof.

Terminal condition. At k=T+1k=T{+}1 the sum is empty (=0=0); the constraint ∑t=T+1Tht=j\sum_{t=T+1}^{T}h_{t}=j requires j=0j=0.

Recursion. Fix k≤Tk\leq T, s,js,j. The first term in the sum (27) is Ck​exp⁡(sk)=Ck​esC_{k}\exp(s_{k})=C_{k}e^{s}. Splitting the minimization by hkh_{k}:

Case hk=0h_{k}=0. The transition gives sk+1=s+δks_{k+1}=s+\delta_{k} and the residual constraint ∑t=k+1Tht=j\sum_{t=k+1}^{T}h_{t}=j. By definition, the inner minimization equals Uk+1​(s+δk,j)U_{k+1}(s+\delta_{k},j), and the branch contributes Ck​es+Uk+1​(s+δk,j)C_{k}e^{s}+U_{k+1}(s+\delta_{k},j).

Case hk=1h_{k}=1. The transition gives sk+1=s+δk/2s_{k+1}=s+\delta_{k}/2 and constraint ∑t=k+1Tht=j−1\sum_{t=k+1}^{T}h_{t}=j-1, requiring j≥1j\geq 1. The branch contributes Ck​es+Uk+1​(s+δk/2,j−1)C_{k}e^{s}+U_{k+1}(s+\delta_{k}/2,j-1) when j≥1j\geq 1 and +∞+\infty otherwise.

Combining the branches gives (28).

Recovery. At k=1,s=0k=1,s=0, equation (27) matches (26) since si,1​(hi)=0s_{i,1}(h_{i})=0. ∎

J.7 Discretization and exact-slope correction

The state ss in (28) is continuous, ranging over [0,smax][0,s_{\max}] with smax:=∑t=1Tδts_{\max}:=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\delta_{t}. We discretize. Construct a uniform grid 𝒢:={s(1),…,s(G)}\mathcal{G}:=\{s^{(1)},\ldots,s^{(G)}\} with s(g)=(g−1)​smax/(G−1)s^{(g)}=(g-1)\,s_{\max}/(G-1), define the snapping operator Π⁡(s):=arg⁡mins′∈𝒢​|s−s′|\Pi(s):=\arg\min_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}}|s-s^{\prime}| (ties broken arbitrarily), and replace the exact transitions s+δks+\delta_{k} and s+δk/2s+\delta_{k}/2 in (28) with Π⁡(s+δk)\Pi(s+\delta_{k}) and Π⁡(s+δk/2)\Pi(s+\delta_{k}/2). The grid Bellman recursion

U~k(s(g),j)=min{\displaystyle\widetilde{U}_{k}(s^{(g)},j)\;=\;\min\!\Bigl\{ Ck​es(g)+U~k+1​(Π⁡(s(g)+δk),j),\displaystyle C_{k}\,e^{s^{(g)}}+\widetilde{U}_{k+1}\bigl(\Pi(s^{(g)}+\delta_{k}),\,j\bigr), (29)
Ckes(g)+U~k+1(Π(s(g)+δk/2),j−1) 1{j≥1}+∞ 1{j=0}},\displaystyle C_{k}\,e^{s^{(g)}}+\widetilde{U}_{k+1}\bigl(\Pi(s^{(g)}+\delta_{k}/2),\,j-1\bigr)\,\mathbf{1}\{j\geq 1\}+\infty\,\mathbf{1}\{j=0\}\,\Bigr\},

with terminal U~T+1​(s(g),0)=0\widetilde{U}_{T+1}(s^{(g)},0)=0 and U~T+1​(s(g),j)=+∞\widetilde{U}_{T+1}(s^{(g)},j)=+\infty for j≥1j\geq 1, can be solved backward in 𝒪⁡(T2​G)\mathcal{O}(T^{2}G) per individual. We also record the optimizing action πk​(g,j)∈{0,1}\pi_{k}(g,j)\in\{0,1\} at each (k,g,j)(k,g,j).

Exact-slope correction.

Reading U~1​(0,j)\widetilde{U}_{1}(0,j) directly off the grid would give approximate slopes with discretization error of order smax/Gs_{\max}/G, propagating into the breakpoints of the lower envelope and corrupting the budget comparison. We use the grid to identify a near-optimal policy, then compute its slope exactly:

  1. 1.

    Forward trace. For each j∈{0,1,…,T}j\in\{0,1,\ldots,T\}, initialize g←1g\leftarrow 1 and jrem←jj_{\text{rem}}\leftarrow j. For k=1,…,Tk=1,\ldots,T: read h^k(j)←πk​(g,jrem)\hat{h}_{k}^{(j)}\leftarrow\pi_{k}(g,j_{\text{rem}}); if h^k(j)=1\hat{h}_{k}^{(j)}=1 update g←Π⁡(s(g)+δk/2)g\leftarrow\Pi(s^{(g)}+\delta_{k}/2) and jrem←jrem−1j_{\text{rem}}\leftarrow j_{\text{rem}}-1, else g←Π⁡(s(g)+δk)g\leftarrow\Pi(s^{(g)}+\delta_{k}). By construction, h^(j)∈{0,1}T\hat{h}^{(j)}\in\{0,1\}^{T} has ‖h^(j)‖1=j\|\hat{h}^{(j)}\|_{1}=j.

  2. 2.

    Exact recompute. Evaluate

    fi,j:=∑t=1TCi,t​exp⁡(∑j′<tδi,j′​(1−h^j′(j)/2)),f_{i,j}\;:=\;\sum_{t=1}^{T}C_{i,t}\,\exp\!\Bigl(\sum_{j^{\prime}<t}\delta_{i,j^{\prime}}\bigl(1-\hat{h}^{(j)}_{j^{\prime}}/2\bigr)\Bigr), (30)

    in continuous arithmetic with no snapping.

The resulting fi,jf_{i,j} may exceed the true minimum on ℋj\mathcal{H}_{j}, but is exact for the policy h^(j)\hat{h}^{(j)}: discretization affects which policy is selected, not its reported objective. The lower envelope built from {fi,j}j=0T\{f_{i,j}\}_{j=0}^{T} via Lemma 2 therefore has exact slopes; only the per-budget policy is approximate. As G→∞G\to\infty, h^(j)\hat{h}^{(j)} converges to the true minimizer of ℋj\mathcal{H}_{j}.

J.8 Algorithm and complexity

The argument leads to the following theorem, which is what Section 5.1 cites.

Theorem 3 (Parametric inner DP).

For each i∈ℐ1i\in\mathcal{I}_{1}, there exist scalars {fi,j}j=0T\{f_{i,j}\}_{j=0}^{T}, depending only on the nuisance fits and the observed data, such that for every BB and every λh\lambda_{h},

minhi∈{0,1}T⁡[V^i​(B,hi)+λh​‖hi‖1]=minj∈{0,1,…,T}⁡[αi​(B)⋅fi,j+λh⋅j],\min_{h_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{T}}\!\bigl[\widehat{V}_{i}(B,h_{i})+\lambda_{h}\,\|h_{i}\|_{1}\bigr]\;=\;\min_{j\in\{0,1,\ldots,T\}}\!\bigl[\alpha_{i}(B)\cdot f_{i,j}\,+\,\lambda_{h}\cdot j\bigr], (31)

with αi​(B)=B⁡(Xi)/[n​(p^Btrl)2]\alpha_{i}(B)=B(X_{i})/[n(\hat{p}_{B}^{\text{trl}})^{2}]. The slopes {fi,j}j=0T\{f_{i,j}\}_{j=0}^{T} are computed by Algorithm 2 in 𝒪⁡(T2​G)\mathcal{O}(T^{2}G) time per individual on a state grid of size GG, and the discretization error in the recovered slopes vanishes as G→∞G\to\infty.

Proof.

The decoupling in Section J.1 together with the arm-collapse and state rewrite in Sections J.2–J.3 yield the per-individual factorization Vitrl​(B,hi)=αi​(B)​∑tCi,t​exp⁡(si,t​(hi))V_{i}^{\text{trl}}(B,h_{i})=\alpha_{i}(B)\sum_{t}C_{i,t}\exp(s_{i,t}(h_{i})) in (23). Lemma 2 then converts the per-individual minimum into the lower envelope on the right-hand side of (31). Proposition 2 expresses fi,j=U1​(0,j)f_{i,j}=U_{1}(0,j) as a backward Bellman recursion, and the discretization-plus-exact-recompute procedure of Section J.7 computes {fi,j}\{f_{i,j}\} exactly along the recovered policies {h^(j)}\{\hat{h}^{(j)}\} at 𝒪⁡(T2​G)\mathcal{O}(T^{2}G) cost per individual; as G→∞G\to\infty, the recovered policies converge to the true minimizers of (26). ∎

Build cost.

The backward pass in Algorithm 2 runs TT stages, each updating G⁡(T+1)G(T+1) table entries with 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) work per entry, for a total of 𝒪⁡(T2​G)\mathcal{O}(T^{2}G). The forward-trace and exact-recompute phase costs 𝒪⁡(T)\mathcal{O}(T) per budget level, summed to 𝒪⁡(T2)\mathcal{O}(T^{2}). Per individual, 𝒪⁡(T2​G)\mathcal{O}(T^{2}G); across the trial sample, 𝒪⁡(n1​T2​G)\mathcal{O}(n_{1}T^{2}G).

Query cost.

Given a candidate BB, the inner-optimal value of V^\widehat{V} is

minh⁡[V^​(B,h)+λh​‖h‖1]=𝒞⁡(B)+∑i∈ℐ1minj=0,…,T⁡[αi​(B)​fi,j+λh​j],\min_{h}\!\bigl[\widehat{V}(B,h)+\lambda_{h}\|h\|_{1}\bigr]\;=\;\mathcal{C}(B)\;+\;\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}\;\min_{j=0,\ldots,T}\!\bigl[\alpha_{i}(B)\,f_{i,j}\,+\,\lambda_{h}\,j\bigr], (32)

where 𝒞⁡(B)\mathcal{C}(B) is the target-side block of (5) and αi​(B)\alpha_{i}(B) is given by (22). Each per-individual minimum requires 𝒪⁡(T)\mathcal{O}(T) scalar operations, giving 𝒪⁡(n1​T)\mathcal{O}(n_{1}T) total per outer-loop query.

Reusability and comparison to a non-parametric DP.

The slopes {fi,j}\{f_{i,j}\} depend only on the nuisance fits, independent of BB and λh\lambda_{h}: Algorithm 2 runs once at the start of the outer loop, and subsequent BB-queries reduce to (32). The same precomputation supports re-querying at different λh\lambda_{h} values via the direct update of intercepts {j​λh}j=0T\{j\lambda_{h}\}_{j=0}^{T}. A naive grid DP on the joint state (s,j)(s,j) that absorbed αi​(B)\alpha_{i}(B) into the per-step cost would have identical 𝒪⁡(T2​G)\mathcal{O}(T^{2}G) build cost but would need to be re-solved for every BB candidate; the parametric formulation factors αi​(B)\alpha_{i}(B) out of the recursion, amortizing the cache across the entire Rashomon ensemble of MM trees. The reduction from "rebuild per BB" to "query per BB" is the main source of computational saving.

Appendix K R-gating: Prioritizing the Censoring Channel

An attribution issue can corrupt h∗h^{*} if applied naively. Theorem 2’s integrand mixes the two red factors multiplicatively, so a unit with very large ℓ​(Xi)2\ell(X_{i})^{2} but only moderate IPCW will still have Δi,k\Delta_{i,k} dominated by the baseline channel. The DP would then activate hi,kh_{i,k} on such a unit even though censoring is not what is inflating its variance. We address this with a soft per-unit gate that downweights hh-eligibility for units whose per-unit variance is baseline-dominated, and keeps it for units where censoring is the larger contributor. The gate is re-drawn between the random tree split comparisons and held fixed across each candidate branch evaluation to keep that comparison on a common gate; a hard gate is applied at aggregation. Operationally, R-gating sharpens the attribution between regions (ii)–(iv) of Section 4.3: hh acts on units whose variance is censoring-driven, while BB absorbs the rest.

K.1 The censoring-amplification factor FiF_{i}

Let Ai∈{0,1}A_{i}\in\{0,1\} be the observed treatment for trial unit ii, and let λka​(x)=Pr⁡(Yk=1∣Yk−1=1,Ck−1=0,X=x,A=a,S=1)\lambda_{k}^{a}(x)=\Pr(Y_{k}=1\mid Y_{k-1}=1,\,C_{k-1}=0,\,X=x,\,A=a,\,S=1) be the per-interval hazard fit on the at-risk set (k=2,…,Tk=2,\dots,T; λ1≡1\lambda_{1}\equiv 1). The conditional survival from kk to TT on arm aa is the backward product

Qka(x)=∏j=k+1Tλja(x),k=0,1,…,T,QTa(x)≡1.Q_{k}^{\,a}(x)\;=\;\prod_{j=k+1}^{T}\lambda_{j}^{a}(x),\qquad k=0,1,\dots,T,\qquad Q_{T}^{\,a}(x)\equiv 1. (33)

Define the per-period variance-increment matrix Qincr∈ℝ≥0n1×TQ_{\mathrm{incr}}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n_{1}\times T} on the observed arm,

Qincr,i,k={(QkAi​(Xi))2−(Qk−1Ai​(Xi))2,k=1,…,T−1,QT−1Ai​(Xi)​(1−QT−1Ai​(Xi)),k=T,Q_{\mathrm{incr},\,i,k}\;=\;\begin{cases}\bigl(Q_{k}^{\,A_{i}}(X_{i})\bigr)^{2}-\bigl(Q_{k-1}^{\,A_{i}}(X_{i})\bigr)^{2},&k=1,\dots,T-1,\\[4.0pt] Q_{T-1}^{\,A_{i}}(X_{i})\bigl(1-Q_{T-1}^{\,A_{i}}(X_{i})\bigr),&k=T,\end{cases} (34)

non-negative for k<Tk<T by the monotonicity Qk−1≤QkQ_{k-1}\leq Q_{k}. Let πCa​(x,k−1)=Pr⁡(Ck=0∣Ck−1=0,Yk−1=1,X=x,A=a,S=1)\pi_{C}^{a}(x,k{-}1)=\Pr(C_{k}=0\mid C_{k-1}=0,\,Y_{k-1}=1,\,X=x,\,A=a,\,S=1) be the per-interval censoring survival probability, and define the log-censoring penalty and its cumulative version

δi,k=− 2logπCAi(Xi,k−1),Σi,k=∑j=1kδi,j(clipped at 50),\delta_{i,k}\;=\;-\,2\log\pi_{C}^{\,A_{i}}\!\bigl(X_{i},\,k-1\bigr),\qquad\Sigma_{i,k}\;=\;\sum_{j=1}^{k}\delta_{i,j}\quad\bigl(\text{clipped at }50\bigr), (35)

so that exp⁡(Σi,k)=∏j=1kπCAi​(Xi,j−1)−2\exp(\Sigma_{i,k})=\prod_{j=1}^{k}\pi_{C}^{\,A_{i}}(X_{i},j-1)^{-2} is the squared cumulative inverse-censoring weight along ii’s observed trajectory through period kk. The censoring-amplification factor is the QincrQ_{\mathrm{incr}}-weighted mean of these squared inverse-censoring weights:

Fi=∑k=1TQincr,i,k​exp⁡(Σi,k)∑k=1TQincr,i,k,F_{i}\;=\;\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{T}Q_{\mathrm{incr},\,i,k}\;\exp\!\bigl(\Sigma_{i,k}\bigr)}{\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{T}Q_{\mathrm{incr},\,i,k}}, (36)

with the denominator floored at 10−1510^{-15} for degenerate at-risk paths. Three properties of FiF_{i} are immediate from (36):

Lower bound at unity.

Since πC≤1\pi_{C}\leq 1 implies δi,k≥0\delta_{i,k}\geq 0 and hence exp⁡(Σi,k)≥1\exp(\Sigma_{i,k})\geq 1, we have Fi≥1F_{i}\geq 1 identically; equality holds when there is no censoring along ii’s trajectory.

Period-weighted average.

FiF_{i} is a convex combination of the per-period squared inverse-censoring weights exp⁡(Σi,k)\exp(\Sigma_{i,k}) with weights Qincr,i,k/∑k′Qincr,i,k′Q_{\mathrm{incr},i,k}/\sum_{k^{\prime}}Q_{\mathrm{incr},i,k^{\prime}}; periods that contribute little to the variance contribute correspondingly little to FiF_{i}.

Multiplier of the time-varying block.

FiF_{i} scales the time-varying (censoring) block of V⁡(B,h)V(B,h) in Theorem 2, in the same way that ℓ​(Xi)2\ell(X_{i})^{2} scales the baseline (transport) block; their ratio is therefore the unit-free, per-individual sensitivity used by the gate.

K.2 Transport-vs.-censoring ratio

For each trial unit i∈{1,…,n1}i\in\{1,\dots,n_{1}\} define

Ri=ℓ​(Xi)2Fi.R_{i}\;=\;\frac{\ell(X_{i})^{2}}{F_{i}}. (37)

By construction ℓ​(Xi)2\ell(X_{i})^{2} is the multiplier of the baseline (time-invariant, transport) block of V⁡(B,h)V(B,h), while Fi≥1F_{i}\geq 1 is the multiplier of the time-varying (censoring) block; their ratio is therefore the unit-free, per-individual sensitivity of the variance to the transport channel relative to the censoring channel. Two reading conventions are used throughout:

  • •

    RiR_{i} large ⇒\;\Rightarrow\; baseline block dominates ⇒\;\Rightarrow\; only BB reduces the contribution of unit ii;

  • •

    RiR_{i} small ⇒\;\Rightarrow\; time-varying block dominates ⇒\;\Rightarrow\; hh reduces the contribution of unit ii without trimming it.

Units with ℓ​(Xi)2/Fi\ell(X_{i})^{2}/F_{i} otherwise non-finite are flagged and treated as “uninformative” (set to the neutral mid-gate value below).

K.3 Soft RR-gate (used inside the Rashomon trees)

Let σ⁡(z)=(1+e−z)−1\sigma(z)=(1+e^{-z})^{-1}, and let m~\widetilde{m} be the empirical median of log⁡R\log R over trial units with finite RiR_{i}:

m~=mediani:Ri​finite(logRi).\widetilde{m}\;=\;\operatorname*{median}_{\,i\,:\,R_{i}\,\text{finite}}\bigl(\log R_{i}\bigr). (38)

The per-unit soft gating probability is the median-centred logistic

phi=pmin+(pmax−pmin)σ(−αgate(logRi−m~)),i=1,…,n1,p_{h}^{\,i}\;=\;p_{\min}\;+\;\bigl(p_{\max}-p_{\min}\bigr)\,\sigma\!\Bigl(-\alpha_{\mathrm{gate}}\,\bigl(\log R_{i}-\widetilde{m}\bigr)\Bigr),\qquad i=1,\dots,n_{1}, (39)

with the convention phi=12p_{h}^{\,i}=\tfrac{1}{2} for any unit with non-finite RiR_{i}. The defaults used in our experiments are (pmin,pmax,αgate)=(0.05, 0.95, 3)(p_{\min},p_{\max},\alpha_{\mathrm{gate}})=(0.05,\,0.95,\,3). Equation (39) has three properties we rely on:

Median-anchored.

phi=pmin+pmax2p_{h}^{\,i}=\tfrac{p_{\min}+p_{\max}}{2} exactly when log⁡Ri=m~\log R_{i}=\widetilde{m}, so the gate is calibrated to the empirical distribution of RR rather than to its absolute scale. Replacing RR by c​RcR for any c>0c>0 shifts m~\widetilde{m} by log⁡c\log c and leaves phip_{h}^{\,i} pointwise unchanged.

Bounded away from {0,1}\{0,1\}.

phi∈[pmin,pmax]⊂(0,1)p_{h}^{\,i}\in[p_{\min},p_{\max}]\subset(0,1), so every unit retains a non-zero inclusion probability across the ensemble; no individual is permanently excluded inside the Rashomon search.

Monotone in RR.

phip_{h}^{\,i} is strictly decreasing in RiR_{i}, so larger transport contribution maps monotonically to smaller hh-inclusion probability.

During tree growth a single Bernoulli draw

Mi(node)∼Bern(phi),i=1,…,n1,M^{\,(\mathrm{node})}_{i}\;\sim\;\mathrm{Bern}\!\bigl(p_{h}^{\,i}\bigr),\qquad i=1,\dots,n_{1}, (40)

is taken once per internal node and shared across all four (bL,bR)∈{0,1}2(b_{L},b_{R})\!\in\!\{0,1\}^{2} candidates evaluated at that node; conditional on Mi(node)=0M^{\,(\mathrm{node})}_{i}=0, the row of the parametric-DP output for unit ii is forced to 𝟎T\mathbf{0}_{T} before the variance evaluator is called. The single-mask invariant (one draw per node, reused across all four candidates) ensures the four-way comparison is not corrupted by mask noise.

K.4 Hard RR-gate (used in the final hh-profile)

After Rashomon aggregation yields B^\widehat{B} (step 5 of Algorithm 3), the parametric DP is queried once at B^\widehat{B} to produce a raw intervention matrix h^raw∈{0,1}n1×T\widehat{h}^{\mathrm{raw}}\in\{0,1\}^{n_{1}\times T}. The reported intervention is then hardened via the median threshold:

h^i,t=h^i,traw{phi≥12}=h^i,traw{logRi≤m~},t=1,…,T.\widehat{h}_{i,t}\;=\;\widehat{h}^{\mathrm{raw}}_{i,t}\,\mathbf{1}\!\bigl\{p_{h}^{\,i}\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\bigr\}\;=\;\widehat{h}^{\mathrm{raw}}_{i,t}\,\mathbf{1}\!\bigl\{\log R_{i}\leq\widetilde{m}\bigr\},\qquad t=1,\dots,T. (41)

The two indicator forms are equivalent because, by (39), phi≥12p_{h}^{\,i}\geq\tfrac{1}{2} iff log⁡Ri≤m~\log R_{i}\leq\widetilde{m}, regardless of (pmin,pmax,αgate)(p_{\min},p_{\max},\alpha_{\mathrm{gate}}) as long as the interval [pmin,pmax][p_{\min},p_{\max}] contains 12\tfrac{1}{2} symmetrically around its midpoint when the midpoint equals 12\tfrac{1}{2}. With the defaults pmin+pmax=1p_{\min}+p_{\max}=1 used above, the hard gate is exactly the median split of log⁡R\log R: hh is allowed to act on the half of the trial units whose variance is censoring-dominated, and is suppressed on the other half.

K.5 Sorting trimmed units by cause: regions (iii) and (iv)

The subgroup underrepresented only at baseline, i.e., trimmed but not censoring-depleted, is of interest because future trials could fix it directly through recruitment. It does not follow directly from the optimum: once a unit is trimmed, its ℓ⁡(X)\ell(X) leaves the summary tree, so hh is not computed for it; regions (iii) and (iv) of Section 4.3 are therefore separated by RiR_{i} rather than by h∗h^{*}, with no new machinery. Before any trimming, TRACE computes the gating statistic Ri=ℓ​(Xi)2/FiR_{i}=\ell(X_{i})^{2}/F_{i} of (37) for every trial unit, where the numerator is the baseline variance inflation and FiF_{i} is the censoring-driven inflation; large RiR_{i} means baseline is the dominant cause and small RiR_{i} means censoring. Gating the trimmed units by RiR_{i} therefore sorts them by cause. On Experiment 2c (baseline and censoring compounding), this separates the baseline-only trims (conceptually B=0B=0, h=0h=0) from the baseline-and-censoring trims (conceptually B=0B=0, h=1h=1) near-perfectly, with AUC 0.990.99 over 10 seeds.

Appendix L TRACE Algorithm

Algorithm 3 summarizes the full nested procedure of Section 5: calibration of λh\lambda_{h}, the inner parametric DP that returns h∗​(B)h^{*}(B) (Appendix J), the Rashomon ensemble over BB, aggregation of the Rashomon set into B∗B^{*}, and the post-hoc RR-gate (Appendix K).

Appendix M Experiments Details

M.1 Experiment 1

Experiment 1 uses ten independent 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1) covariates. X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} affect both trial participation and the survival hazard, X3X_{3} and X4X_{4} affect censoring, and X5,…,X10X_{5},\ldots,X_{10} are noise. The trial-participation model is calibrated so that the expected trial-to-target ratio is about 2:12{:}1; the resulting transport weight ℓ⁡(X)\ell(X) ranges over roughly 10−2.610^{-2.6} to 101.910^{1.9}. Censoring depends on X3X_{3} and X4X_{4} as follows. Individuals with high X3X_{3} but not high X4X_{4} (about 23%23\% of the sample) have an early, moderate censoring spike over t∈{3,4,5}t\in\{3,4,5\} with peak hazard κ=0.30\kappa=0.30; individuals with high X4X_{4} but not high X3X_{3} (about 17%17\%) have a late, heavy spike over t∈{7,8,9}t\in\{7,8,9\} with peak hazard κ=0.75\kappa=0.75; all other individuals have the baseline censoring hazard κ=0.05\kappa=0.05 at every interval. The late spike is 2.52.5 times as strong as the early one by design: an early spike inflates the cumulative IPCW product at every later interval, whereas a late spike acts on an at-risk set that earlier events have already thinned, so the design tests whether hh correctly gives more weight to early censoring. We use T=10T=10 follow-up intervals, n=5,000n=5{,}000 individuals, randomized binary treatment in the trial, 1,0001{,}000 Rashomon trees with K=30K=30 retained within an objective tolerance of 3.03.0, and λh\lambda_{h} calibrated to a 5%5\% intervention rate (η=0.95\eta=0.95).

Results.

Three patterns are expected by design and a fourth is not. (i) BB splits only on the participation covariates X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} and trims the high-ℓ\ell tail, while hh acts only on the censoring covariates X3X_{3} and X4X_{4}; the noise covariates X5,…,X10X_{5},\ldots,X_{10} are used by neither intervention. (ii) The summary tree for h∗​(B)h^{*}(B) recovers the two spike windows: a tight peak near t=4t=4 for the high-X3X_{3} subgroup and a wider, later peak near t=7t=7 for the high-X4X_{4} subgroup. (iii) hh assigns comparable numbers of person-intervals to the early and late spike subgroups (3030 and 2424) despite the late spike’s 2.52.5 times larger peak hazard, consistent with early censoring inflating the cumulative IPCW product at all later intervals. (iv) A fourth leaf concentrates on individuals with both high X3X_{3} and high X4X_{4}, who receive only baseline censoring yet are intervened at both spike windows; the algorithm produced this leaf from the variance contributions alone.

M.2 Experiments 2a–2d

Experiments 2a–2d isolate the two mechanisms in a two-covariate setting: baseline underrepresentation only (2a), time-varying underrepresentation only (2b), both at once on different covariates (2c), and an adversarial case in which the underrepresented region consists of two corners that no single axis-aligned split can recover (2d). Together with Experiment 1, the designs follow prior generalizability and transportability simulation studies (Parikh et al., 2025), extended with the survival and censoring structure.

Common setup.

Each replication draws n=5,000n=5{,}000 subjects with covariates X=(X1,X2)⊤∼𝒩⁡(0,I2)X=(X_{1},X_{2})^{\top}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{2}) and follows them over T=6T=6 intervals. Trial membership is drawn from Pr⁡(S=1∣X)=σ⁡(ξ0+sel⁡(X))\Pr(S=1\mid X)=\sigma(\xi_{0}+\mathrm{sel}(X)), where σ\sigma is the logistic function, the selection function sel⁡(⋅)\mathrm{sel}(\cdot) is specific to each experiment, and the intercept ξ0\xi_{0} is chosen numerically so that 𝔼⁡[Pr⁡(S=1∣X)]=2/3\mathbb{E}[\Pr(S=1\mid X)]=2/3, giving about 3,3003{,}300 trial and 1,7001{,}700 target subjects per replication. The censoring hazard is κ⁡(X,t)=0.05\kappa(X,t)=0.05 at every interval except t=3t=3, where it equals κspike\kappa_{\mathrm{spike}} on an experiment-specific region (no spike in 2a). We ran TRACE at both κspike∈{0.30,0.85}\kappa_{\mathrm{spike}}\in\{0.30,0.85\} and under two alternative normalizations of the empirical objective in addition to the block-self-normalized objective of Section 4.2 (Appendix H); Figure 2 reports the block-self-normalized objective at κspike=0.85\kappa_{\mathrm{spike}}=0.85.

Experiment 2a (baseline underrepresentation only).

sel⁡(X)=1.5​X1\mathrm{sel}(X)=1.5\,X_{1}, so ℓ⁡(X)\ell(X) is large for small X1X_{1}, and censoring is uniformly mild (κspike=0.05\kappa_{\mathrm{spike}}=0.05, i.e., no spike). The only excess variance comes from the covariate shift on X1X_{1}.

Experiment 2b (time-varying underrepresentation only).

sel⁡(X)=0.1​X1\mathrm{sel}(X)=0.1\,X_{1}, so ℓ⁡(X)\ell(X) is nearly uniform, with a strong censoring spike at t=3t=3 on the half-plane {X2<0}\{X_{2}<0\}. The excess variance comes from the spike region, not from trial-target mismatch.

Experiment 2c (both mechanisms).

sel⁡(X)=1.5​X1\mathrm{sel}(X)=1.5\,X_{1} as in 2a, combined with the censoring spike of 2b on {X2<0}\{X_{2}<0\} at t=3t=3. The two mechanisms act on different covariates, so both trimming and hh are needed, and neither substitutes for the other.

Experiment 2d (adversarial case).

sel⁡(X)=−2.0​c⁡(X)\mathrm{sel}(X)=-2.0\,\sqrt{c(X)} with corner score

c⁡(X)=max⁡{(−X1−0.5)​(X2−0.5), 0}+max⁡{(X1−0.5)​(−X2−0.5), 0},c(X)\;=\;\max\!\bigl\{(-X_{1}-0.5)(X_{2}-0.5),\,0\bigr\}\;+\;\max\!\bigl\{(X_{1}-0.5)(-X_{2}-0.5),\,0\bigr\},

which makes trial participation rare, and ℓ⁡(X)\ell(X) large, in the upper-left and lower-right corners of the (X1,X2)(X_{1},X_{2}) plane, a region that no single axis-aligned split can recover; the censoring spike at t=3t=3 is on {X1+X2<0}\{X_{1}+X_{2}<0\}, a direction not aligned with the corners.

TRACE configuration.

The trim function BB is a tree of maximum depth 66 for Experiments 2a–2c and depth 1010 for 2d (the corners require deeper splits). We grow 1,0001{,}000 trees, retain the K=30K=30 near-optimal trees within an objective tolerance of 3.03.0, and aggregate BB by 2/32/3-majority vote. The censoring intervention h∈{0,1}ntrl×Th\in\{0,1\}^{n_{\mathrm{trl}}\times T} is selected by the parametric DP of Appendix J, and λh\lambda_{h} is calibrated to a 5%5\% intervention rate (η=0.95\eta=0.95) by the quantile rule of Section 4.2.

Appendix N Quantitative Recovery Metrics for the Synthetic Experiments

Precision and recall are not uniquely defined for underrepresentation, because “underrepresented” needs a ground truth that the DGP does not directly yield. For instance, one may use ℓ⁡(X)\ell(X) as a metric for baseline underrepresentation, but any cutoff (e.g., ℓ⁡(X)>1\ell(X)>1, >3>3, or >10>10) is a choice we impose, not a fact of the DGP. Moreover, ℓ⁡(X)\ell(X) alone does not characterize baseline underrepresentation: a sample with small ℓ⁡(X)\ell(X) but large heterogeneity is still underrepresented but not flagged by such a cutoff (Section 3.3). We nevertheless report precision and recall, together with hh interval localization and the noise-split rate, for all five DGPs against the following imperfect ground truth.

Table 1 defines the ground truth and the metrics. The intervened region is read from a depth-2 summary tree fit to the TRACE output (BB: on target units to the trim label; hh: on trial units to receiving any gated hh).

Results.

Table 2 reports means and standard deviations over 10 seeds at n=5,000n=5{,}000 with 1,0001{,}000 trees and K=30K=30. Across the BB metrics (Table 2a), recall stays at 1.001.00 for the axis-aligned DGPs (2a, 2c) at every cutoff while precision changes as the cutoff varies, so the precision values are set by the arbitrary cutoff, not by the method. For hh (Table 2b), precision is high on Experiments 2b–2d (0.870.87–1.001.00), TRACE recovers much of the censoring region (recall up to 0.900.90 on 2d), and it places interventions on the exact spike interval 8787–97%97\% of the time. The hard case is Experiment 1, where the two censoring subgroups are defined by X3X_{3} and X4X_{4} jointly (high X3X_{3} but not X4X_{4}, and high X4X_{4} but not X3X_{3}), a pattern that a shallow summary tree cannot trace exactly, so hh precision falls to 0.660.66 (0.770.77 on TRACE’s raw interventions, before tree summarization). This is a limit of the tree summary rather than of TRACE, as hh localization remains high at 94%94\%. On Experiment 1, none of the 2323 BB splits and 22 of the 3030 hh splits fall on a noise covariate.

Appendix O Comparison with Simpler Diagnostic Baselines

We compare TRACE with four simpler diagnostics on Experiment 2c, where baseline and censoring underrepresentation compound on different covariates: ℓ\ell-thresholding, censoring-thresholding, combined-thresholding, and ROOT applied to ℓ\ell (Table 3). Direct IPCW thresholding is not a valid censoring diagnostic, because the IPCW is cumulative and propagates across time; a thresholding rule must integrate the whole trajectory, which is what our DP for hh does, so censoring-thresholding is implemented through two DP variants, with and without the ℓ​(X)2\ell(X)^{2} weight. Only TRACE attributes the two mechanisms correctly and identifies where extrapolation is unreliable.

Appendix P JTPA-to-CPS Case Study: Data, Harmonization, and Configuration

This appendix supplies the implementation detail behind the JTPA-to-CPS analysis of Section 7: the construction of the trial and target samples, the harmonization rules that align their covariates, the outcome and follow-up encoding, the missing data handling, the TRACE hyperparameters, and the full numerical results that the main text reports only in compressed form.

P.1 Data availability

Both data sources used in this case study are public-use files released by federally sponsored research archives, and no restricted-use, contractual, or fee-bearing access is required to reproduce the analysis.

JTPA Study.

The National Job Training Partnership Act Study public-use file is distributed by the W.E. Upjohn Institute for Employment Research and is mirrored at the Inter-university Consortium for Political and Social Research (“National JTPA Study: Impacts, Costs, and Benefits”) (Bloom et al., 1997). The file contains the randomization assignment, the baseline covariates listed in Appendix P.4, and the monthly employment and follow-up records used to construct the time-to-employment outcome of Appendix P.5. Registration with ICPSR is free and open to all researchers.

CPS-ASEC.

The March 1988 Annual Social and Economic Supplement to the Current Population Survey is released by the U.S. Census Bureau and the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and is available without restriction through two harmonized public repositories: IPUMS-CPS at the Minnesota Population Center (Flood et al., 2022), which we used for the harmonized variable extracts, and the CEPR Uniform CPS Extracts maintained by the Center for Economic and Policy Research (Center for Economic and Policy Research, 2019), which we used to cross-validate the labor-force and demographic codings. The era-matching rule (March 1988 ASEC matched to calendar year 1987) follows the standard practice for this survey wave.

Reproducibility artifact.

The harmonization scripts, TRACE configuration files, and analysis code that map the two public-use sources to the analytic samples and figures of Section 7 are released with this paper as supplementary material.

P.2 Trial cohort: JTPA

The trial sample is drawn from the National Job Training Partnership Act (JTPA) Study (Bloom et al., 1997; Abadie et al., 2002), a multi-site randomized experiment that offered eligible adult applicants either access to or denial of federally funded job-training services. Two restrictions are imposed at intake. First, we keep only individuals with valid randomization records, which removes a small number of units whose treatment assignment cannot be verified against site logs. Second, we require baseline unemployment at the randomization date, since the estimand of Section 7 is time-to-employment and units already employed at t=0t=0 contribute no follow-up information for the survival outcome. After these restrictions, the analytic trial cohort has n1=10,379n_{1}=10{,}379 adults, with treatment assignment Ai∈{0,1}A_{i}\in\{0,1\} recording the offer of training. Randomization is conducted within site–cohort strata, and we treat the marginal Pr⁡(A=1∣X,S=1)\Pr(A=1\mid X,S=1) as known by design and equal to its empirical value within strata.

P.3 Target cohort: CPS-ASEC, era-matched

The target sample is drawn from the March 1988 Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC) of the Current Population Survey (Flood et al., 2022; Center for Economic and Policy Research, 2019), era-matched to calendar year 1987 to align with the JTPA randomization window and to avoid confounding by macroeconomic drift between the trial period and the target frame. We apply a four-step inclusion funnel that mirrors the JTPA eligibility rule:

  1. 1.

    Age window. Restrict to ages 2222–6565, matching the JTPA adult eligibility band.

  2. 2.

    Not employed. Drop respondents employed at the reference week, parallel to the trial-side baseline-unemployment restriction in Appendix P.2.

  3. 3.

    Out-of-scope reasons. Remove respondents whose reason for not working in the prior year was retirement, illness or disability, or school attendance, which lie outside the JTPA-eligible adult population.

  4. 4.

    Labor-force attachment. Retain respondents who are unemployed (looking for work) at the reference week or who worked at some point in 1987.

After the funnel, the target sample comprises n0=7,630n_{0}=7{,}630 individuals (3,1293{,}129 unemployed at the reference week and 4,5014{,}501 out of the labor force but with work in 1987), representing approximately 1212 million U.S. JTPA-eligible adults under the CPS-ASEC person weights. We use the unweighted CPS sample for nuisance fitting and reweight to the ASEC weights at the estimand level via standard post-stratification.

P.4 Covariate harmonization

We harmonize nine baseline covariates that are recorded in both data sources but with different coding conventions: age (years), sex (female indicator), Black, Hispanic, married, an indicator for high school diploma or GED, years of completed education, previous annual earnings (USD), and hourly wage at last job (USD). We note three harmonization rules. First, education is retained both as years and as a high-school-or-GED indicator because JTPA records the GED separately from the standard high-school diploma whereas CPS-ASEC collapses both under the same diploma flag; carrying both encodings preserves the resolution of the trial side without inducing CPS imputation error. Second, earnings and wages are deflated to constant 1987 dollars using the CPI-U-RS index and are top-coded at the CPS-side cap to avoid distributional artifacts at the right tail. Third, race-ethnicity is encoded as two non-overlapping indicators (Black, Hispanic) with non-Hispanic White as the reference category; respondents identifying with multiple groups are assigned to the most-cited bridge category in the CPS documentation, and JTPA records are mapped to the same bridge.

P.5 Outcome and follow-up encoding

The outcome of interest is an indicator that the participant was employed in any month during months 11 through 2424 post-randomization. We convert this to a discrete-time survival representation by treating “first employment” as the event and right-censoring at month 2424 for participants who do not become employed during follow-up. Concretely, for each trial unit ii we define T=24T=24 monthly intervals, with Yi,t+1=1Y_{i,t+1}=1 if ii is not yet employed by month t+1t+1 (still at risk for the event) and Yi,t+1=0Y_{i,t+1}=0 once employment is observed. The censoring indicator Ci,tC_{i,t} records loss to follow-up at interval tt, which in JTPA arises from administrative reasons such as residential moves, refusal to complete the follow-up survey, or interview non-response, and is observed conditional on prior at-risk status. We adopt the standard convention C¯−1=0\bar{C}_{-1}=0 and Y0=1Y_{0}=1.

P.6 Missing-data handling

Item-level missingness in the harmonized covariates is moderate (below 7%7\% on every variable except previous earnings, which is missing for 11.4%11.4\% of JTPA records). We impute missing covariates by single chained-equations imputation using mice (van Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011) with 2020 iterations, predictive mean matching for continuous variables, and logistic regression for binary variables. We do not impute the outcome or censoring indicators, which are observed by design on the trial side and not defined on the target side.

P.7 TRACE configuration

We run TRACE with the configuration of Section 4, specialized to the JTPA-to-CPS scale as follows. The Rashomon ensemble grows M=1,000M=1{,}000 axis-aligned trees over the union of trial and target individuals, with maximum depth 66, a minimum leaf size of 200200, and an objective tolerance of 3.03.0 that defines the near-optimal set; the top K=30K=30 trees within tolerance form the retained ensemble, and B∗B^{*} is aggregated by 2/32/3-majority vote across the set. Nuisance functions ℓ^\hat{\ell}, π^a\hat{\pi}^{a}, π^C,ja\hat{\pi}^{a}_{C,j}, and Q^ka\hat{Q}^{a}_{k} are fitted by gradient-boosted trees on five-fold cross-fits, with hyperparameters tuned by held-out log-loss on the trial side and held-out classification accuracy on the source classifier Pr^​(S=0∣X)\hat{\Pr}(S=0\mid X). The censoring penalty λh\lambda_{h} is calibrated to the default sparsity level η=0.95\eta=0.95 via the empirical-quantile rule of Section 4.2, and R-gating (Appendix K) is applied at 30%30\% refinement to sharpen the attribution between the baseline and censoring channels. The inner DP runs on a state grid of size G=256G=256, which produces slope errors below 10−410^{-4} in absolute terms on the JTPA-scale problem.

P.8 Numerical results

Variance contraction.

The TRACE objective drops from V^​(𝟏,𝟎)=81.58\widehat{V}(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{0})=81.58 at the no-trim baseline to V^​(B∗,h∗)=12.68\widehat{V}(B^{*},h^{*})=12.68 at the optimum, an 84.5%84.5\% reduction. The Rashomon set is confined to [13.13, 13.77][13.13,\,13.77], indicating that the variance landscape is flat near the optimum and that the diagnostic identification is robust to the specific tree selected from the ensemble. The supermajority 2/32/3-vote rule trims 46.3%46.3\% of the target sample and 13.8%13.8\% of the trial sample, with the trim regions concentrated on higher-socioeconomic-status profiles common in CPS but rare in JTPA.

Attribution.

The censoring intervention h∗h^{*} activates on 9898 of 249,096249{,}096 trial person-intervals (0.04%0.04\%), compared with 1,7961{,}796 activations in the same configuration with R-gating disabled. The contrast indicates that the variance inflation in JTPA-to-CPS is predominantly baseline-driven: hh absorbs only the residual that remains once BB has trimmed the baseline mismatch, and even that residual is concentrated on a small number of person-intervals. Decomposing the empirical sum of the trial-side red-factor product ℓ​(X)2/π¯C,t−1a​(X)2\ell(X)^{2}/\bar{\pi}^{a}_{C,t-1}(X)^{2}, the contribution contracts from 1.47×1061.47\times 10^{6} at the baseline to 2.28×1052.28\times 10^{5} at the optimum (a 6.4×6.4\times reduction), while the target-centering block remains roughly four orders of magnitude smaller throughout, consistent with the long horizon T=24T=24 at which the outcome variance is dominated by the trial-side IPCW inflation.

Effect-estimate precision.

The point estimate is −τ^24-\hat{\tau}_{24}=+0.034=+0.034 (standard error SE^=0.027\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}=0.027), and the 95%95\% confidence interval contracts from the no-trim [−10.5,+15.9][-10.5,\,+15.9] percentage points to [−1.9,+8.6][-1.9,\,+8.6] percentage points, a 60.6%60.6\% reduction in width. Although the contracted interval still includes zero, it is now narrow enough to bound the population-level effect on the 2424-month employment rate within an ≈10\approx 10-percentage-point window, which is policy-relevant for prioritizing JTPA-style training programs across the JTPA-eligible adult population.

Localization of underrepresentation (Figure 3).

The BB-tree trims four higher-socioeconomic-status branches: previous earnings ≥$8,922\geq\$8{,}922 and married; previous earnings ≥$14,000\geq\$14{,}000 and unmarried; previous earnings <$8,922<\$8{,}922 with ≥14\geq 14 years of education and married; and a small residual leaf combining moderate earnings and high education. The retained region corresponds to the typical disadvantaged-adult profile (previous earnings <$8,922<\$8{,}922 and <14<14 years of education), consistent with the JTPA selection rule. Within the much smaller censoring-depleted region, the dominant hh-active leaf groups individuals with previous earnings <$2,148<\$2{,}148 and ages 2424–4242 (n=3,954n=3{,}954), which alone carries about 80%80\% of all h∗h^{*} activations. This leaf’s activations are sharply peaked at t=21t=21, with 4545 of the leaf’s 5050 interventions falling in that single month, which we interpret as a late-second-year loss-to-follow-up shock that selectively depletes the most informative trial subgroup. JTPA generalizability therefore fails through two channels: the trial is over-concentrated on the most disadvantaged enrollees relative to the CPS target (the where and the baseline why), with a residual late-window attrition channel that depletes low-earnings young adults during the second year of follow-up (the when and the temporal why).

P.9 Sensitivity to tuning parameters

We assess the sensitivity of the JTPA diagnosis along the hh-sparsity quantile (η∈{0.85,0.9,0.95}\eta\in\{0.85,0.9,0.95\}), the Rashomon ensemble size (M∈{200,400,600}M\in\{200,400,600\}) and set size (K∈{5,10,30}K\in\{5,10,30\}), the soft RR-gate steepness (αgate∈{1,3,5}\alpha_{\mathrm{gate}}\in\{1,3,5\}), the hard RR-gate refinement (bottom 30%30\% vs. 50%50\%), the positivity floor (Pr⁡(S=1∣X)<{0.01,0.05,0.1}\Pr(S{=}1\mid X)<\{0.01,0.05,0.1\}), the maximum tree depth ({4,6,8}\{4,6,8\}), the minimum leaf size ({25,50,100}\{25,50,100\}), and the DP grid size (G∈{25,50,100}G\in\{25,50,100\}). The reference setting is η=0.95\eta=0.95, floor 0.050.05, αgate=3\alpha_{\mathrm{gate}}=3, hard gate 30%30\%, M=600M=600, K=30K=30, depth 66, minimum leaf size 5050, and G=50G=50, at which the objective falls from V^​(𝟏,𝟎)=81.57\widehat{V}(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{0})=81.57 to V^​(B,h)=14.36\widehat{V}(B,h)=14.36. Agreement between the regions recovered under different settings is summarized by the Jaccard index |A∩B|/|A∪B||A\cap B|/|A\cup B| of the trimmed target sets (for BB) or of the sets of trial units receiving a gated hh (for hh). Table 5 summarizes the sweeps. Across all assessed parameters, the optimized variance V^​(B,h)\widehat{V}(B,h) and the recovered regions are stable. The soft RR-gate is insensitive by design, since it always applies hh to censoring-dominated units and never to baseline-dominated ones, with αgate\alpha_{\mathrm{gate}} setting only the sharpness of the transition; the hard RR-gate is applied to the final summary tree, so it leaves BB unchanged and only admits more hh interventions, and the near-invariance of the variance when it admits four times as many is itself evidence that baseline underrepresentation, not censoring, dominates. In summary, the JTPA conclusion is robust to the considered tuning parameters, and the invariance of V^​(B,h)\widehat{V}(B,h) to the hh-related parameters is consistent with baseline underrepresentation being the dominant mechanism.

Appendix Q Compute Resources

All experiments run on a single workstation with an AMD Ryzen 9 5950X 16-core CPU and no GPU acceleration. The Rashomon ensemble parallelizes directly over the MM independent trees, and we use all 16 cores throughout. End-to-end wall-clock times for the M=1,000M=1{,}000-tree TRACE configurations reported in the paper are approximately 60−9060-90 minutes for the synthetic experiments (Section 6: n=5,000n=5{,}000, T∈{6,10}T\in\{6,10\}, two-covariate or ten-covariate DGPs) and approximately 44 hours for the JTPA-to-CPS case study (Section 7: n1=10,379n_{1}=10{,}379, n0=7,630n_{0}=7{,}630, T=24T=24, nine harmonized covariates with five-fold cross-fit nuisances). The longer JTPA runtime reflects the longer follow-up horizon, the larger covariate space, and the gradient-boosted-tree nuisance estimation step. Memory usage stays under 1616 GB for both settings.

Computational complexity.

The cost of TRACE has two parts: a one-time parametric DP build, then many cheap searches, so the DP is never rerun at each tree split. The DP precomputes the per-unit budget envelopes in 𝒪⁡(ntrl​T2​G)\mathcal{O}(n_{\mathrm{trl}}\,T^{2}G); after that, each tree-split search costs only 𝒪⁡(ntrl​T)\mathcal{O}(n_{\mathrm{trl}}\,T). Growing the Rashomon ensemble takes about 𝒪⁡(M​ 2D​F)\mathcal{O}(M\,2^{D}F) splits for MM depth-DD trees over FF covariates, for a total of 𝒪⁡(ntrl​T2​G+M​ 2D​F​ntrl​T)\mathcal{O}(n_{\mathrm{trl}}\,T^{2}G+M\,2^{D}F\,n_{\mathrm{trl}}\,T). The expensive T2​GT^{2}G term is incurred once and never compounds with the 2D2^{D} tree term, which is what keeps the JTPA-scale configuration of Appendix P.7 within the wall-clock times reported above.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

  1. 1.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: The abstract and Section 1 state three contributions. Contribution 1 (variance decomposition isolating baseline and time-varying mechanisms) is supported by Theorem 1, with the (B,h)(B,h)-parametrized extension in Theorem 2. Contribution 2 (variance-minimization with self-regulating constraint) is supported by Theorem I.1 and the empirical objective in Section 4.2. Contribution 3 (parametric DP nested in a Rashomon ensemble) is realized by Algorithm 3. Empirical claims are supported by the synthetic results in Section 6 and the JTPA-to-CPS results in Section 7.

    Limitations

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: Section 8 contains a dedicated Limitations paragraph. TRACE is diagnostic, not corrective. It identifies subgroups for whom generalization is unreliable but does not adjust the point estimator, and the BB-restricted estimand differs from the original PATE, so practitioners must report this shift. We also note there that inference for the BB-restricted PATE does not account for the data-driven selection of (B,h)(B,h).

The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting.       It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.

    • •

      It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

    • •

      For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

    • •

      If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

  36. 8.

    Experiments compute resources

  37. Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments?

  38. Answer: [Yes]

  39. Justification: All experiments run on a single CPU workstation (16-core AMD Ryzen 9 5950X, no GPU, no cluster). End-to-end wall-clock for the M=1,000M=1{,}000-tree TRACE configuration is approximately 60−9060-90 minutes for the synthetic experiments and approximately 44 hours for the JTPA-to-CPS case study, with peak memory under 1616 GB (Appendix Q). The Rashomon ensemble parallelizes directly over the MM trees, and the asymptotic compute cost of the inner DP is established in Theorem 3 (𝒪⁡(T2​G)\mathcal{O}(T^{2}G) per individual on a state grid of size GG; Appendix J).

  40. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.

    • •

      The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute.

    • •

      The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper).

  41. 9.

    Code of ethics

  42. Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines?

  43. Answer: [Yes]

  44. Justification: The research conforms to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics (https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines); we use only de-identified public-use survey data (JTPA, CPS-IPUMS, and CEPR extracts), preserve participant anonymity in reporting, and identify no dual-use risks specific to the diagnostic released.

  45. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

    • •

      If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.

    • •

      The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction).

  46. 10.

    Broader impacts

  47. Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

  48. Answer: [Yes]

  49. Justification: Section 8 contains a Limitations, future work, and broader impacts paragraph in which we discuss positive impacts (transparent diagnostics for whom RCT-based decisions can be reliably extrapolated to, supporting equity in evidence-based policy) and risks of misuse (confusing the trim and hh-intervention outputs with causal claims about trimmed subgroups), and recommend reporting trimmed-region characteristics alongside the diagnostic as a mitigation.

  50. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

    • •

      If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

    • •

      Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

    • •

      The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

    • •

      The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

    • •

      If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

  51. 11.

    Safeguards

  52. Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)?

  53. Answer: [N/A]

  54. Justification: The paper does not release any high-risk pretrained models, generative models, or scraped datasets. The released artifacts are diagnostic code only, applied to public-use survey data.

  55. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks.

    • •

      Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.

    • •

      Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.

    • •

      We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.

  56. 12.

    Licenses for existing assets

  57. Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected?

  58. Answer: [Yes]

  59. Justification: JTPA public-use data (Bloom et al., 1997) are accessed under the NBER public-use terms, and CPS data are accessed under the IPUMS-CPS terms of use (Flood et al., 2022) and the CEPR uniform-extracts terms (Center for Economic and Policy Research, 2019); all are credited in Section 7 and Appendix P. The mice R package (van Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011) is used under its GPL (≥2\geq 2) license as distributed on CRAN.

  60. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets.

    • •

      The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset.

    • •

      The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL.

    • •

      The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset.

    • •

      For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided.

    • •

      If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset.

    • •

      For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided.

    • •

      If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators.

  61. 13.

    New assets

  62. Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets?

  63. Answer: [Yes]

  64. Justification: The TRACE diagnostic code is released as a supplementary archive with a README documenting entry points, expected inputs, and outputs for the DGP simulators, the Rashomon-tree fitter, the inner DP, the TMLE pipeline, and the post-hoc R-gating routines. A data-card-style description of the JTPA-to-CPS preprocessing pipeline accompanies the code.

  65. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets.

    • •

      Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc.

    • •

      The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used.

    • •

      At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file.

  66. 14.

    Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects

  67. Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)?

  68. Answer: [N/A]

  69. Justification: The paper performs secondary analysis of de-identified public-use survey data (JTPA and CPS); no crowdsourcing was used and no original human-subjects data collection was performed.

  70. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper.

    • •

      According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector.

  71. 15.

    Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects

  72. Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained?

  73. Answer: [N/A]

  74. Justification: The paper performs secondary analysis of de-identified public-use survey data and does not involve original human-subjects research; IRB approval is therefore not applicable.

  75. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper.

      We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution.

      For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review.

    Declaration of LLM usage

  77. Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required.
